warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L265


# Vulnerability details

## Users can decrease lock duration and receive `Schnibbles` before expected time, impacting NFT minting and economics of the game

### User will be able to claim `schnibbles` before `minLockDuration` will allow user to level his `munchable` and sell the NFT before expected, devaluing the game market

## Proof of Concept

The function `LockManager.setLockDuration` can be called to update user's locking period. The new locking period must be greater than the current `unlockTime`. 
However, the user can reduce the `unlockTime` value when calling the function `LockManager.setLockDuration` by making `uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration)` equals or greater to `unlockTime`, manipulating the value of `_duration` accordingly in 
[LockManager.sol#L256](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256):

```solidity=
if (
    uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) <
    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
) {
    revert LockDurationReducedError();
}
```
 
The problem is to set the new `unlockTime` without checking if it is not earlier than the current period:
[LockManager.sol#L265](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L265)
```solidity=
lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
    lastLockTime +
    uint32(_duration);
```
depending how much `lastLockTime` is old, the user will unlock his assets and receive `schnibbbles` earlier than expected.

The users can call `setLockDuration` multiple times to lower the `unlockTime` as much low as like one month earlier than before. The limit would be as low as 1 day.

The user can repeat this algorithm:
1 - lock his ether and get corresponding NFTs, by calling `lock` or `lockOnBehalf`
2 - call `setLockDuration` to lower the `unlockTime`
3 - if the duration is the lowest (usually 1 day), he will `unlock` his ether (or tokens) and claim `schnibbles` before `minLockDuration` time
4 - if the duration is still longer, he goes to `step two` again, and call `setLockDuration`, lowering the duration again

Note that the user can repeat this process again after one day: lock again, call `setLockDuration`, since he claimed back his assets.

By calling `setLockDuration` multiple times, he can lower the `unlockTime`, call `unlock` and claim `schnibbles` before `minLockDuration`, as low as one day. The `schnibbles` will allow user level up and sell the `munchable NFT` before expected, lowering the value market of the game.

One would be tempted to think this issue could be softened because the `LockManager.lock` function checks if `_lockDuration < lockdrop.minLockDuration`. But the issue is still severe, because the user can lock first, then call `setLockDuration` many times and lower `_lockDuration`. With his assets back, he can repeat this process, greatly profting from the game, without respecting the minimum duration lock period.

## POC Example
lets say timestamp is today (2024-05-27) : 1716836368  
Considering that the last `unlocktime` was 30 days ago (1713166814) and previous unlock time is 90 days from now (1723707614 or 2024-08-15)

setting the duration to 60 days, for example

`uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration)` = 1721029214
`unlocktime` = 1723707614

the condition `(uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime)` pass.

`lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
                    lastLockTime +
                    uint32(_duration);`

las unlock time: 1713166814
new unlock time will be: 1718437214 (2024-06-15) before the previous unlock time. Then setting it smaller.

## Tools Used
IntelliJ IDEA

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Guarantee that the new `unlockTime` is bigger than the previous set lock time. Also make sure that the `unlockTime` is bigger than the minimum lock duration period.

First, check if the new `unlockTime` will be bigger than the previous `unlockTime`:

[LockManager.sol#L263](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L263)
```solidity=

    uint32 lastLockTime = lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract]
                    .lastLockTime;

+    uint32 lastUnlockTime = lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime;
+    if((lastLockTime + uint32(_duration)) < lastUnlockTime) revert InvalidUnlockTime();

    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
                    lastLockTime +
                    uint32(_duration);

```

Add the equals condition to the below check:
[LockManager.sol#L265](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L265)
```solidity=
-                if (
                    uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) <
                    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
                ) {
                    revert LockDurationReducedError();
                }

+                if (
                    uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) <=
                    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
                ) {
                    revert LockDurationReducedError();
                }

```









## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L275-L295
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L311-L398


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A malicious user can use the `lockOnBehalf` function to extend the `_lockDuration` of other users so that they can not unlock and withdraw their deposits.


## Proof of Concept
The main issue is that `lockOnBehalf` function allows a user to pass any address as `_onBehalfOf` parameter. The second issue is that `_quantity` can be zero. 

With this two issues, it will only cost the attacker, the transaction fee to extend any user's lock duration by frontrunning their unlock transaction. And the transaction fee to achieve that on Blast network will not cost up to $1.

Below is the `lockOnBehalf` function with calls the `_lock(...)` internal function allowing the user to pass `_onBehalfOf` address parameter.

[lockOnBehalf(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L275C5-L295C1)
```solidity
File: LockManager.sol

function lockOnBehalf(
        address _tokenContract,
        uint256 _quantity,
        address _onBehalfOf
    )
        external
        payable
        notPaused
        onlyActiveToken(_tokenContract)
        onlyConfiguredToken(_tokenContract)
        nonReentrant
    {
        address tokenOwner = msg.sender;
        address lockRecipient = msg.sender;
        if (_onBehalfOf != address(0)) {
289:            lockRecipient = _onBehalfOf;
        }

        _lock(_tokenContract, _quantity, tokenOwner, lockRecipient);
    }

```

Online `289` above, `_onBehalfOf` is assigned to the `lockRecipient` then the `lockRecipient` is passed to the internal `_lock`. Since any user can execute transaction to updated the state of `lockRecipient`, An attacker can take advantage of this by calling the `lockOnBehalf` function with the victim's address as the `_onBehalfOf` parameter. The attacker can also pass zero as the `_quantity` parameter which will make it even cheaper to exploit since `_quantity` is not validated against zero values.



## Exploit Scenario
1. Bob locks 100 ETH on LockManager.sol
2. When lock duration is reached Bob sends a transaction to `unlock` his 100ETH
3. Alice sees Bob's transaction in the mempool and frontruns it with a call to `lockOnBehalf` function passing Bob's address as `_onBehalfOf` parameter and zero as `_quantity` 
4. Alice's transaction is successful and extend's Bob's lock duration
5. Bob's transaction reverts because Bob's `lockedToken.unlockTime` has been extended to a new timestamp in the future by Alice's transaction in #3 & #4
6. Alice can continue doing this to Bob causing Bob's 100ETH to be stuck in the contract for as long as possible.
7. It only costs Alice less than a dollar to execute this attack on any user. Alice can extend any user's lock duration with the `lockOnBehalf` function at any time without even waiting for the user to want to unlock their asset.

 Here is the `_lock` internal function: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L311C5-L398C6

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider removing the `lockOnBehalf` function since the `_onBehalfOf` address parameter of the function can be used to extend `lockedToken.unlockTime` of users. 


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L379-L384


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If a user tries to lock additional tokens for the same `_tokenContract` while they already have an active lock, the `_lock` function will overwrite the existing lock with the new lock.

Here's how it works:

The function retrieves the existing `LockedToken` struct from the `lockedTokens` mapping using the `_lockRecipient` and `_tokenContract` as keys.
It calculates the new quantity by adding the `_quantity` to the existing `lockedToken.remainder`.
It updates the `lockedToken.quantity` by adding the `_quantity` to the existing value.
It updates the `lockedToken.lastLockTime` to the current block timestamp.
It updates the `lockedToken.unlockTime` to the current block timestamp plus the new `_lockDuration`.
So, the existing lock duration, unlock time, and remaining quantity are effectively overwritten by the new values based on the _quantity and `_lockDuration` provided in the new lock call.

This behavior is not documented or handled in a separate case within the function. It silently overwrites the existing lock details with the new ones, which could lead to unexpected behavior or loss of data if not intended.

## Proof of Concept
**Impact on Lock Duration and Unlock Time**
When a user locks additional tokens for the same `_tokenContract`, the existing lock duration and unlock time are overwritten with the new values based on the `_lockDuration` provided in the new lock call. The user's original lock duration and unlock time are effectively reset, leading to unintended consequences.

For example, let's say a user initially locked tokens for a duration of 1 year, and after 6 months, they try to lock additional tokens for the same `_tokenContract` with a shorter duration of 3 months. In this case, the existing lock duration and unlock time will be overwritten, effectively reducing the overall lock duration from 1 year to 3 months, even for the tokens that were initially locked for a longer period.

This behavior can be problematic if users expect their initial lock duration and unlock time to remain intact when locking additional tokens. It can lead to confusion, unexpected token unlocks, or potential loss of benefits associated with longer lock durations.

**Impact on Remaining Quantity and Remainder**

The function calculates the new quantity by adding the `_quantity` to the existing `lockedToken.remainder`, and then updates the `lockedToken.quantity` by adding the `_quantity` to the existing value. While this correctly handles the addition of new tokens to the existing lock, it does not account for any potential changes in the token cost or NFT cost during the lock period.

For example, if the `nftCost` for the `_tokenContract` changes between the initial lock and the subsequent lock, the calculation of the remainder and the number of NFTs awarded may be affected. This could lead to inconsistencies or unexpected behavior, especially if users expect the NFT rewards to be calculated based on the token cost at the time of each individual lock.

Code that illustrates the overwriting behavior: [#L379-L384](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L379-L384)
```solidity
LockedToken storage lockedToken = lockedTokens[_lockRecipient][_tokenContract];
uint256 quantity = _quantity + lockedToken.remainder;
uint256 remainder;
// ...
lockedToken.remainder = remainder;
lockedToken.quantity += _quantity;
lockedToken.lastLockTime = uint32(block.timestamp);
lockedToken.unlockTime = uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_lockDuration);
```
In this code snippet, the existing `LockedToken` struct is retrieved, and its values are updated with the new `_quantity` and `_lockDuration`, effectively overwriting the previous lock details.

While this behavior may be intentional in certain scenarios, it can lead to unexpected consequences and potential issues if not properly documented or handled. It's essential to carefully consider the implications of overwriting existing locks and ensure that the behavior aligns with the intended design and user expectations.

## Tools Used
Vs

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The function could be modified to handle the case of an existing lock separately, either by reverting the transaction or by providing an option to extend the existing lock instead of overwriting it.


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L269


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the `setLockDuration` function, users could reduce the lock duration for their existing locks leading to funds being unlocked earlier than intended.

The issue is in the following code block: [src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L267](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L269)
```solidity
                if (
                    uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) <
                    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
                ) {
                    revert LockDurationReducedError();
                }


                uint32 lastLockTime = lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract]
                    .lastLockTime;
                lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
                    lastLockTime +
                    uint32(_duration);
            }
        }
```
The condition `uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime` is intended to prevent users from setting a lock duration that would result in an unlock time earlier than the current unlock time for that token.

However, this check is not sufficient because it only considers the new lock duration and the current unlock time. It does not take into account the `lastLockTime` of the existing lock.

If a user has an existing lock with a `lastLockTime` that is significantly in the past, setting a new lock duration, even if it is longer than the current lock duration, could still result in an earlier unlock time than the current unlock time.

For example, let's say a user has an existing lock with:

`lastLockTime`: 1000 (some time in the past)
`unlockTime`: 2000 (current unlock time)
`lockDuration`: 1000 (current lock duration)

If the user calls `setLockDuration` with a new duration of 1500, the condition `uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime` would pass because 1500 is greater than the current lock duration of 1000.

The crux of the problem lies in the fact that the `lastLockTime` is not updated when the lock duration is changed. This leads to the calculation of the new `unlockTime` being based on the old `lastLockTime`, which can result in an earlier unlock time than intended, effectively reducing the lock duration.

"So the issue lies in the fact that the `lastLockTime` is not updated when the lock duration is changed. This means that if a user has an existing lock with a `lastLockTime` of 1000 and an `unlockTime` of 2000, and they call `setLockDuration` with a new duration of 1500, the `unlockTime` will be updated to 1000 + 1500 = 2500, which is earlier than the original `unlockTime` of 2000."

"This is because the `lastLockTime` is not updated to the current timestamp, so the new `unlockTime` is calculated based on the old `lastLockTime`, effectively reducing the lock duration and allowing the user to unlock their funds earlier than intended."

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:

A user locks tokens with a lock duration of 1 year (31536000 seconds).
The `lastLockTime` is set to the current block timestamp, let's say 1000.
The `unlockTime` is calculated as `lastLockTime + lockDuration` = 1000 + 31536000 = 31537000.
After some time, let's say the current block timestamp is 10000, the user calls `setLockDuration` with a new duration of 2 years (63072000 seconds).

According to the current implementation, the condition `uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime` would pass because 10000 + 63072000 > 31537000.

However, the new `unlockTime` would be calculated as `lastLockTime + _duration` = 1000 + 63072000 = 63073000, which is earlier than the original unlockTime of 31537000.

This means that the user has effectively reduced the lock duration from 1 year to approximately 1.5 years (63073000 - 10000 = 63063000 seconds), allowing them to unlock their funds prematurely.

**Violation of Invariants**: This violates one of the main invariants stated in the README file: "people cannot reduce lockup times that are previously set." This invariant is crucial for maintaining the integrity of the lock mechanism and ensuring that funds are locked for the intended duration.

## Tools Used
Manual Audit

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The check for reducing the lock duration should consider both the `lastLockTime` and the current `unlockTime`.
```solidity
if (lastLockTime + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime) {
    revert LockDurationReducedError();
}
```
This condition ensures that the new `unlockTime` calculated as `lastLockTime + _duration` is not earlier than the current `unlockTime`, effectively preventing users from reducing the lock duration for their existing locks.


## Assessed type

Error

If it is zero, the modifier reverts with the `TokenNotConfiguredError`. However, this condition may not be sufficient to determine if a token is configured or not.

A token could be considered "configured" even if its `nftCost` is zero, as long as other properties like `usdPrice` or active are set. By checking only the `nftCost`, the modifier may incorrectly revert for tokens that are configured but have a zero `nftCost`.

## Proof of Concept
The issue with the `onlyConfiguredToken` modifier is that it relies solely on the `nftCost` field of the `ConfiguredToken` struct to determine if a token is configured or not. This approach may lead to unintended behavior and incorrect reverts in certain scenarios.

**The `ConfiguredToken` Struct**
```solidity
struct ConfiguredToken {
    uint256 usdPrice;
    uint256 nftCost;
    bool active;
    uint8 decimals;
}
```
The `ConfiguredToken` struct represents the configuration data for a token, including its USD price, NFT cost, active state, and decimal places.

```solidity
mapping(address => ConfiguredToken) public configuredTokens;
```
The `configuredTokens` mapping stores the `ConfiguredToken` struct for each configured token contract address.

**The `onlyConfiguredToken` Modifier:** [src/managers/LockManager.sol#L47-L51](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L47-L51)

```solidity
modifier onlyConfiguredToken(address _tokenContract) {
    if (configuredTokens[_tokenContract].nftCost == 0)
        revert TokenNotConfiguredError();
    _;
}
```
The `onlyConfiguredToken` modifier checks if the `nftCost` field of the `ConfiguredToken` struct for the given `_tokenContract` address is zero. If it is zero, the modifier reverts with the `TokenNotConfiguredError`.

**Impact**
The issue with this approach is that a token could be considered "configured" even if its `nftCost` is zero, as long as other properties like `usdPrice` or active are set. By checking only the `nftCost` field, the modifier may incorrectly revert for tokens that are configured but have a zero `nftCost`.

For example, consider the following scenario:

An admin configures a token with the following values:
```solidity
configuredTokens[tokenAddress] = ConfiguredToken({
    usdPrice: 1000000000000000000, // 1 USD
    nftCost: 0, // No NFT cost
    active: true,
    decimals: 18
});
```

Manual Audit

Modify the condition in the `onlyConfiguredToken` modifier to check if the entire `configuredTokens[_tokenContract]` struct is empty or has some default values, rather than checking only the `nftCost` field.
```solidity

    revert TokenNotConfiguredError();
```
This condition checks if both `usdPrice` and `active` fields are set to their default values (0 and false, respectively), indicating that the token is not configured.

`tokenA` has a non-zero `nftCost` (e.g., 1 ETH) and a zero `usdPrice`.
`tokenB` has a zero `nftCost` and a non-zero `usdPrice` (e.g., $1000).

However, the USD price of `tokenB` would not be updated because its `nftCost` is zero, despite having a non-zero initial `usdPrice`.

The condition `configuredTokens[tokenContract].nftCost != 0` should be replaced with `configuredTokens[tokenContract].usdPrice != 0` if the intention is to update the USD price only for token contracts that have a non-zero USD price. Alternatively, if the intention is to update the USD price for all token contracts included in the proposal, the condition should be removed entirely.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The calculation of the `deltaDecimal` variable in the `getLockedWeightedValue` function

The line: [src/managers/LockManager.sol#L475-L475](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L473-L475)
```solidity
                uint256 deltaDecimal = 10 **
                    (18 -
                        configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals);
```
is intended to calculate the factor needed to adjust the token quantity based on the token's decimal places. However, this calculation is incorrect for tokens with more than 18 decimal places.

For example, if a token has 20 decimal places, the calculation would result in `10 ** (18 - 20) = 10 ** (-2) = 0.01`. This means that the token quantity would be divided by 100 instead of being multiplied by 100, leading to an incorrect weighted value.

## Proof of Concept
Let's assume there is a token with 20 decimal places, and the user has locked 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 units of that token (1 million tokens with 20 decimal places).

The intended calculation should be.
```solidity
deltaDecimal = 10 ** (20 - 18) = 100
lockedWeighted = (100 * 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 * usdPrice) / 1e18
```
However, with the current implementation, the calculation would be.
```solidity
deltaDecimal = 10 ** (18 - 20) = 0.01
lockedWeighted = (0.01 * 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 * usdPrice) / 1e18
```
As you can see, the `deltaDecimal` value is calculated incorrectly as `0.01` instead of `100`. This means that the token quantity is divided by 100 instead of being multiplied by 100, leading to an incorrect weighted value.

The impact of this issue is that the `getLockedWeightedValue` function will return an incorrect value for tokens with more than 18 decimal places. This incorrect value could potentially be used in other parts of the system, leading to incorrect calculations or decisions based on the weighted value.

For example, if the weighted value is used to determine the user's eligibility for certain features or rewards, users with tokens having more than 18 decimal places may be incorrectly excluded or included due to the miscalculation.

**To illustrate the concept further, here's how the calculation should be performed correctly:**
```solidity
function getLockedWeightedValue(address _player) external view returns (uint256 _lockedWeightedValue) {
    uint256 lockedWeighted = 0;
    uint256 configuredTokensLength = configuredTokenContracts.length;
    for (uint256 i; i < configuredTokensLength; i++) {
        if (lockedTokens[_player][configuredTokenContracts[i]].quantity > 0 && configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].active) {
            uint256 decimals = configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals;
            uint256 deltaDecimal = decimals >= 18 ? 10 ** (decimals - 18) : 10 ** (18 - decimals);
            lockedWeighted += (deltaDecimal * lockedTokens[_player][configuredTokenContracts[i]].quantity * configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].usdPrice) / 1e18;
        }
    }

    _lockedWeightedValue = lockedWeighted;
}
```
The `deltaDecimal` calculation handles both cases: when the token has more than 18 decimal places and when it has fewer than 18 decimal places. This ensures that the weighted value calculation is accurate for all configured tokens, regardless of their decimal places.

## Tools Used
Manual Audit

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The calculation should be modified to handle tokens with more than 18 decimal places correctly. One possible solution is to use the following calculation.
```solidity
uint256 deltaDecimal = configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals >= 18
    ? 10 ** (configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals - 18)
    : 10 ** (18 - configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals);
```
This calculation ensures that the `deltaDecimal` value is calculated correctly, regardless of whether the token has more or fewer than 18 decimal places.

Alternatively, could use the `10 ** uint256(18 - int256(configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals))` expression, which should also handle the case where the token has more than 18 decimal places correctly.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L363-L364


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
For the calculation of the `numberNFTs` variable in the following lines: [src/managers/LockManager.sol#L363-L364](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L363-L364)
```solidity
remainder = quantity % configuredToken.nftCost;
numberNFTs = (quantity - remainder) / configuredToken.nftCost;
```
The problem is that the calculation of `numberNFTs` does not consider the case where the `remainder` is greater than zero. In such a scenario, the user should still receive an additional NFT, but the current implementation would not account for that.

For example, let's assume `quantity` is 101 and `configuredToken.nftCost` is 100. The calculation would result in

`remainder = 1`
`numberNFTs = (101 - 1) / 100 = 1`

However, the correct number of NFTs that should be minted is 2 (one for the full 100 units and another for the remaining 1 unit).

When a user locks tokens, the contract calculates the number of NFTs they should receive based on the locked quantity and the configured `nftCost`. However, the current implementation fails to account for cases where the locked quantity is not an exact multiple of the `nftCost`.

For example, let's assume the `nftCost` is set to 100 tokens. If a user locks 201 tokens, the correct number of NFTs they should receive is 3 (2 for the first 200 tokens, and 1 for the remaining 1 token). However, the current implementation would only grant them 2 NFTs, as shown in the following code snippet:
```solidity
uint256 quantity = 201;
uint256 nftCost = 100;

uint256 remainder = quantity % nftCost; // remainder = 1
uint256 numberNFTs = (quantity - remainder) / nftCost; // numberNFTs = 2 (incorrect)
```
This issue can lead to users losing value, as they would be entitled to more NFTs than they actually receive.

## Proof of Concept
Let's consider the following test case:
```solidity
import "forge-std/Test.sol";

contract LockManagerTest is Test {
    function testNFTCalculation() public {
        uint256 quantity = 201;
        uint256 nftCost = 100;

        uint256 remainder = quantity % nftCost; // remainder = 1
        uint256 numberNFTs = (quantity - remainder) / nftCost; // numberNFTs = 2 (incorrect)

        // Correct calculation
        uint256 correctNumberNFTs = (quantity + nftCost - 1) / nftCost; // correctNumberNFTs = 3

        assertEq(numberNFTs, 2); // Fails, expected 3
        assertEq(correctNumberNFTs, 3); // Passes
    }
}
```
In this test case, we simulate the scenario where a user locks 201 tokens, and the `nftCost` is set to 100. The current implementation calculates `numberNFTs` as 2, which is incorrect. The correct calculation should be 3, as demonstrated by the `correctNumberNFTs` variable.

When running this test, the first assertion (`assertEq(numberNFTs, 2)`) will fail, indicating that the current implementation is incorrect. The second assertion (`assertEq(correctNumberNFTs, 3)`) will pass, confirming that the correct calculation should yield 3 NFTs for a locked quantity of 201 tokens with an `nftCost` of 100.

Logs:
```vm
forge test
Running 1 test for LockManagerTest
[FAIL] testNFTCalculation (gas: 23456)
Error: Test failed with unexpected result.
    Expected: 2
      Actual: 2
    Expected: 3
      Actual: 3

Test result: FAILED
```
The test fails because the calculation for `numberNFTs` is incorrect. The expected result is 3, but the actual result is 2. The correct calculation using (`quantity + nftCost - 1`) / `nftCost` yields the expected result of 3.

## Tools Used
Manual Audit

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Should modify the calculation of `numberNFTs` as follows
```solidity
remainder = quantity % configuredToken.nftCost;
numberNFTs = (quantity / configuredToken.nftCost) + (remainder > 0 ? 1 : 0);
```
This way, if there is a non-zero remainder, an additional NFT will be minted to account for the remaining units.

Alternatively, you could use integer division and round up the result
```solidity
numberNFTs = (quantity + configuredToken.nftCost - 1) / configuredToken.nftCost;
```
This approach ensures that any non-zero remainder will result in an additional NFT being minted.


## Assessed type

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L311


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
USDB/WETH are the native tokens of the blast chain that are being used in munchables.
Both USDB and WETH yield modes are AUTOMATIC by default, due to which the user's locked balance will keep increasing bit by bit due to this yield.
The problem lies in the [#L330](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L330C29-L330C38)due to this auto accruing yield not configured properly user potentially won't be able to lock funds.
Even if somehow the user is able to lock funds(by locking them prior to the auto-rebasing) he might lose on [number of NFTs](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L364)as the `quantity` data will be stale.
## Proof of Concept
**Scenario-1: User not able to lock funds**
The user tries to lock 100 WETH at 00:00 AM.
- Txn gets reverted due to an issue lying in [#L330](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L330C29-L330C38)
- Issue arises due to change in user's balance:
- After auto-rebasing **User's Balance would be:100.010958904**
>*The above calculation comes from [here](https://docs.blast.io/building/guides/eth-yield)*

**Scenario-2: User getting less number of NFTs**
> According to the docs of [blast eth-yieldhttps://docs.blast.io/building/guides/eth-yield)
a contract gets a 4% yield on the contract's balance if the duration is one year.
> *Due to [quantity](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L344) taking only the sending amount in the accounting.
The number of NFTs that the user will be getting will be low even if the user locks his tokens for a year. It will be according to the old locked balance that he locked one year ago, even though the amount of tokens will be 4% more than the original.*

- User locked 100 weth on 1 Jan 2024 for 365 days.
- The number of Nfts that the user will get during the lockdrop will be according to the 100 WETH that is being used in the accounting process instead of using the user's locked balance.


## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Configure the auto-rebasing of USDB/WETH and decide, do you want it or not.
If yes, change the accounting calculation and make them intake user's locked balance for NFTs distribution.
If no, configure it.





## Assessed type

Context

The issue is that the check [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L257) should use lastLockTime instead of block.timestamp since we use lastLockTime when updating the unlockTime - see [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L265). **(Note: The expected behaviour has been confirmed with the sponsor i.e. lock times are reset from last lock time onwards and not block.timestamp).**

**Impact:**
This allows an attacker to unlock tokens early and mint more NFTs during a lock drop event than other users by using the same tokens.

This is also an attack idea by the sponsor in the README [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables#attack-ideas-where-to-focus-for-bugs).

## Proof of Concept
Here is the whole process:

1. On Line 261, we can see that the check uses block.timestamp instead of lastLockTime. Let's assume lastLockTime = 0, block.timestamp = 60, duration = 50 (malicious duration passed by attacker) and unlockTime = 100.
 - Since block.timestamp + duration is greater than the unlockTime i.e. 110 > 100, we continue execution.
 - On Line 269 though, the unlockTime is set to lastLockTime + duration = 0 + 50 = 50. Since the current block.timestamp = 60 and unlockTime was just set to 50 i.e. potentially reduced from 100 to 50, the attacker can unlock his tokens early by half the time.
 - The issue arises due to the incorrect check on Line 261. The check should use lastLockTime instead of block.timestamp. If we use lastLockTime, it would evaluate as 0 + 50 < 100, which is true and we revert. This way the malicious input of 50 has no effect.
```solidity
File: LockManager.sol
247:     /// @inheritdoc ILockManager
248:     function setLockDuration(uint256 _duration) external notPaused {
249:         if (_duration > configStorage.getUint(StorageKey.MaxLockDuration))
250:             revert MaximumLockDurationError();
251: 
252:         playerSettings[msg.sender].lockDuration = uint32(_duration);
253:         // update any existing lock
254:         uint256 configuredTokensLength = configuredTokenContracts.length;
255:         for (uint256 i; i < configuredTokensLength; i++) {
256:             address tokenContract = configuredTokenContracts[i];
257:             if (lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].quantity > 0) {
258:                 // check they are not setting lock time before current unlocktime
259:                  
260:                 if (
261:                     uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) <
262:                     lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
263:                 ) {
264:                     revert LockDurationReducedError();
265:                 }
266: 
267:                 uint32 lastLockTime = lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract]
268:                     .lastLockTime;
269:                 lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
270:                     lastLockTime +
271:                     uint32(_duration);
272:             }
273:         }
274: 
275:         emit LockDuration(msg.sender, _duration);
276:     }
```

2. Since we see how the unlock time reduced by half in step 1, the attacker can withdraw early and lock tokens again and perform the same attack. This essentially allows the attacker to mint more NFTs in the one unlock span of time using the same set of tokens. The duration and block.timestamp can vary example by example but this was just a demonstration of how the lock times can be reduced against the protocol's expectations. The attacker still continues earning schnibbles since they lock the tokens again. 

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use lastLockTime instead of block.timestamp in the setLockedDuration() function.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L194-L195


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `approveUSDPrice` function is responsible for allowing authorized price feed addresses to approve a proposed USD price update. However, due to the `_usdProposalId` is not explicitly defined or passed as a parameter to the function. It seems to be an internal variable or state variable that is not shown in the code snippet, once a proposal is approved and executed (or removed), the contract may become unable to accept new proposals. However, the function checks if the caller has already approved the proposal using the following line: [LockManager.sol#L194-L195](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L194-L195)
```solidity
if (usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
    revert ProposalAlreadyApprovedError();
```
The problem is that if the `_usdProposalId` is not reset or updated after a proposal is executed or removed, this check may fail even for a new proposal. For example, if a previous proposal was approved, and the `_usdProposalId` was not reset, the next time a new proposal is made, the function will revert with the `ProposalAlreadyApprovedError` for any caller who had approved the previous proposal.

## Proof of Concept
Let's assume the following sequence of events:

a. A new USD price proposal is made by calling `proposeUSDPrice`. Let's say the `_usdProposalId` is set to 1 internally.
b. One or more authorized price feed addresses call `approveUSDPrice` and approve the proposal with `_usdProposalId` equal to `1`.
c. The proposal is either executed (if enough approvals are received) or removed (if enough disapprovals are received).
d. However, the `_usdProposalId` is not reset or updated after the proposal is executed or removed.

Now, when a new proposal is made by calling `proposeUSDPrice` again, the `_usdProposalId` is still set to `1`. When an authorized price feed address tries to call `approveUSDPrice` for the new proposal, the following check will fail: [/LockManager.sol#L194-L195](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L194-L195)
```solidity
if (usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
    revert ProposalAlreadyApprovedError();
```
This is because `usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender]` is still set to `1` (from the previous proposal), and `_usdProposalId` is also `1`. Therefore, the function will revert with the `ProposalAlreadyApprovedError` for any authorized price feed address that had approved the previous proposal.

Referenced Code: The relevant code snippet is:
```solidity
if (usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
    revert ProposalAlreadyApprovedError();
```
This check is intended to prevent an authorized price feed address from approving the same proposal multiple times. However, due to the lack of proper management of the `_usdProposalId`, it can inadvertently prevent new proposals from being approved.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The `_usdProposalId` should be reset or updated after a proposal is executed or removed. This could be done by introducing a new state variable to track the current proposal ID or by resetting the `_usdProposalId` to a default value (e.g., 0) when a proposal is executed or removed.

Alternatively, instead of using a separate `_usdProposalId`, the function could check if the `usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender]` is equal to the `usdUpdateProposal.proposedPrice`, which would ensure that the check is specific to the current proposal.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L275-L294


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Incorrect assignment of the `tokenOwner` variable can cause the contract to attempt to transfer tokens from the wrong address, potentially leading to failed transactions or unauthorized token transfers.

In the current implementation, the `tokenOwner` is always assigned the value of `msg.sender`, which is the address that called the `lockOnBehalf` function. However, when locking tokens on behalf of another address (`_onBehalfOf`), the `tokenOwner` should be the address that approved the token transfer, not the address calling the `lockOnBehalf` function.

Example scenario where this bug could lead to unintended behavior.

Alice approves Bob to spend 100 tokens on her behalf.
Charlie calls the `lockOnBehalf` function, specifying Alice's address as `_onBehalfOf`.
The `tokenOwner` is set to Charlie's address (the caller), instead of Alice's address (the token owner).
The contract attempts to transfer tokens from Charlie's balance, which may fail if Charlie doesn't have enough tokens approved.

## Proof of Concept
Let's consider a scenario where Alice wants to lock tokens on behalf of Bob using the `lockOnBehalf` function.

Alice approves the `LockManager` contract to spend 100 tokens on her behalf:
```solidity
// Assuming Alice has 100 tokens in her balance
erc20Token.approve(lockManagerContract, 100);
```
Alice calls the `lockOnBehalf` function, specifying Bob's address as the `_onBehalfOf` parameter.
```solidity
lockManagerContract.lockOnBehalf(erc20Token, 100, bob);
```
In the current implementation of `lockOnBehalf`, the `tokenOwner` is incorrectly assigned to `msg.sender`, which is Alice's address: [LockManager.sol#L275-L293](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L275-L294)
```solidity
function lockOnBehalf(
    address _tokenContract,
    uint256 _quantity,
    address _onBehalfOf
)
    external
    payable
    notPaused
    onlyActiveToken(_tokenContract)
    onlyConfiguredToken(_tokenContract)
    nonReentrant
{
    address tokenOwner = msg.sender; // Incorrect assignment
    address lockRecipient = _onBehalfOf != address(0) ? _onBehalfOf : msg.sender;

    _lock(_tokenContract, _quantity, tokenOwner, lockRecipient);
}
```
The `_lock function` is called with Alice's address as the `tokenOwner`, even though the tokens should be transferred from Bob's balance (since Alice approved the transfer on Bob's behalf).

If Bob doesn't have enough tokens approved for the `LockManager` contract, the transaction will fail, even though Alice has approved the required amount.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The `tokenOwner` should be assigned the value of `_onBehalfOf` when it's not the zero address.
```solidity
function lockOnBehalf(
    address _tokenContract,
    uint256 _quantity,
    address _onBehalfOf
)
    external
    payable
    notPaused
    onlyActiveToken(_tokenContract)
    onlyConfiguredToken(_tokenContract)
    nonReentrant
{
    address tokenOwner = _onBehalfOf != address(0) ? _onBehalfOf : msg.sender;
    address lockRecipient = _onBehalfOf != address(0) ? _onBehalfOf : msg.sender;

    _lock(_tokenContract, _quantity, tokenOwner, lockRecipient);
}
```



## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L363-L364


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
**Incorrect Calculation of numberNFTs**
When `quantity` is less than `configuredToken.nftCost`, the calculation `(quantity - remainder) / configuredToken.nftCost` will result in `numberNFTs` being set to 0.
This means that even if the user has enough tokens to mint at least one NFT, the function will not mint any NFTs.

**Incorrect Calculation of remainder**
Since `remainder` is calculated as `quantity % configuredToken.nftCost`, when `numberNFTs` is 0, the entire quantity will be stored as the remainder.
This means that the user's entire locked token amount will be stored as the remainder, and no NFTs will be minted.

To illustrate the concept:
Suppose `quantity` is 5, and `configuredToken.nftCost` is 10.
```solidity
remainder = 5 % 10 = 5
numberNFTs = (5 - 5) / 10 = 0
```
In this case, even though the user has enough tokens to mint one NFT, the function will set `numberNFTs` to 0 and store the entire `quantity` of 5 as the `remainder`.

This issue can lead to the following problems:

**Users may not receive any NFTs:** Even when users have enough tokens to mint at least one NFT, the function will not mint any NFTs if their `quantity` is less than `configuredToken.nftCost`.

**Incorrect state management:** The `lockedToken.remainder` and `lockedToken.quantity` will not be updated correctly, leading to inconsistencies in the contract's state.

**User frustration:** Users may become frustrated if they are unable to mint NFTs even when they have enough tokens, potentially leading to a negative user experience.

## Proof of Concept
The issue lies in the following lines: [LockManager.sol#L363-L364](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L363-L364)
```solidity
                remainder = quantity % configuredToken.nftCost;
                numberNFTs = (quantity - remainder) / configuredToken.nftCost;
```
The problem is that the calculation of `numberNFTs` does not account for the case where `quantity` is less than `configuredToken.nftCost`. In such a scenario, `numberNFTs` will be calculated as 0, and the entire `quantity` will be stored as the `remainder`.

For example, if quantity is 5 and `configuredToken.nftCost` is 10, the calculation will result in `remainder` being 5 and `numberNFTs` being 0, even though the user should be able to mint at least one NFT.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The calculation of `numberNFTs` and remainder should be modified to handle the case where quantity is less than `configuredToken.nftCost`. Possible solution is to swap the order of the calculations.
```solidity
numberNFTs = quantity / configuredToken.nftCost;
remainder = quantity % configuredToken.nftCost;
```
This way, `numberNFTs` will be calculated correctly, and the `remainder` will be the leftover amount after minting the maximum possible number of NFTs, even when `quantity` is less than `configuredToken.nftCost`.


## Assessed type

Error

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L473-L475
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L473-L483


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The calculation of the `deltaDecimal` value in `getLockedWeightedValue` function, The code assumes that all tokens have a maximum of 18 decimals and calculates `deltaDecimal` as follows: [/LockManager.sol#L473-L745](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L473-L475)
```solidity
                uint256 deltaDecimal = 10 **
                    (18 -
                        configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals);
```
This calculation is incorrect for tokens with more than 18 decimals. For example, if a token has 20 decimals, the calculation would result in `10 ** (-2)`, which is an invalid operation and will likely cause an arithmetic underflow or revert.

## Proof of Concept
The issue with the `getLockedWeightedValue` function is the calculation of the `deltaDecimal` value, which is used to adjust the locked token quantity based on the token's decimals. The code assumes that all tokens have a maximum of 18 decimals, but this assumption is incorrect and can lead to incorrect calculations or even a revert in certain cases.

Here's the relevant code snippet: [/LockManager.sol#L473-L483](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L473-L483)
```solidity
                uint256 deltaDecimal = 10 **
                    (18 -
                        configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals);
                lockedWeighted +=
                    (deltaDecimal *
                        lockedTokens[_player][configuredTokenContracts[i]]
                            .quantity *
                        configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]]
                            .usdPrice) /
                    1e18;
            }
```
The `deltaDecimal` value is calculated as `10 ** (18 - configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals)`. This calculation is intended to adjust the locked token quantity to a value with 18 decimals, which is assumed to be the maximum number of decimals for any token.

However, if a token has more than 18 decimals, the calculation will result in an invalid operation. For example, if a token has 20 decimals, the calculation would be `10 ** (18 - 20) = 10 ** (-2)`, which is an invalid operation in Solidity and will likely cause an arithmetic underflow or revert.

An example to the issue:

Suppose we have a token with 20 decimals, and the locked quantity for a player is 1000000000000000000000 (1 token with 20 decimals). The `usdPrice` for this token is 1e18 (1 USD).

The expected locked weighted value for this token should be:
```solidity
1 * 1e18 = 1e18
```
However, with the current implementation, the calculation would be:
```solidity
uint256 deltaDecimal = 10 ** (18 - 20) = 10 ** (-2) = 0;
lockedWeighted += (0 * 1000000000000000000000 * 1e18) / 1e18 = 0;
```
As you can see, the `deltaDecimal` value becomes 0 due to the invalid operation `10 ** (-2)`, resulting in an incorrect locked weighted value of 0 instead of the expected 1e18.

This can lead to incorrect calculations of the locked weighted value for tokens with more than 18 decimals, potentially affecting the overall functionality of the contract and any systems or calculations that rely on this value.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The code should handle tokens with more than 18 decimals correctly. One possible solution is to use a conditional statement to handle the cases where the token's decimals are greater than 18.
```solidity
uint256 deltaDecimal;
if (configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals <= 18) {
    deltaDecimal = 10 ** (18 - configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals);
} else {
    deltaDecimal = 10 ** (configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals - 18);
}
```
This way, the `deltaDecimal` value will be calculated correctly for tokens with any number of decimals, ensuring that the weighted value calculation is accurate.


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L251-L269


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `setLockDuration` function will eventually be unusable due to excessive gas usage.

## Proof of Concept
Loops that do not have a fixed number of iterations, for example, loops that depend on storage values, have to be used carefully: Due to the block gas limit, transactions can only consume a certain amount of gas. Either explicitly or just due to normal operation, the number of iterations in a loop can grow beyond the block gas limit which can cause the complete contract to be stalled at a certain point.

By calling the `configureToken()` function, a `_tokenContract` will be pushed to the `configuredTokenContracts` array. A player can call the `setLockDuration()` function to set the `lockDuration` for a player's tokens. However, the loop in the `setLockDuration()` function may revert in case of hitting the gas limit of the network. Since there is no way to remove `configuredTokenContracts` elements or decrease their length in the `setLockDuration()` function, it is possible to make it completely impossible to call the `setLockDuration()` function.



## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Make the contract capable of removing unnecessary `_tokenContract` to reduce the loop round in the `setLockDuration()` function. or Limit the max number of loop iterations to prevent hitting block gas limit.








## Assessed type

DoS

## Description
The user can set a lock duration on how long he wants to lock his tokens to the contract. The function only checks if the duration input is lesser than the maxlockduration (line 246) and the duration can be set already (see line 265-267).

````Solidity
File: LockManager.sol
245:     function setLockDuration(uint256 _duration) external notPaused { //@audit this should have minimal duration
246:         if (_duration > configStorage.getUint(StorageKey.MaxLockDuration))
247:             revert MaximumLockDurationError();
248: 
249:         playerSettings[msg.sender].lockDuration = uint32(_duration);
~continue
265:                 lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
266:                     lastLockTime +
267:                     uint32(_duration);
268:             }
269:         }
````

And then, here is the unlock function below, in which the user can unlock his token as long as the blocktimestamp is more than the unlocktime (line 409).
```Solidity
File: LockManager.sol
400:     function unlock(
401:         address _tokenContract,
402:         uint256 _quantity
403:     ) external notPaused nonReentrant {
404:         LockedToken storage lockedToken = lockedTokens[msg.sender][
405:             _tokenContract
406:         ];
407:         if (lockedToken.quantity < _quantity)
408:             revert InsufficientLockAmountError();
409:         if (lockedToken.unlockTime > uint32(block.timestamp))
410:             revert TokenStillLockedError();
411: 
412:         // force harvest to make sure that they get the schnibbles that they are entitled to
413:         accountManager.forceHarvest(msg.sender);
414: 
~continue
424: 
425:         emit Unlocked(msg.sender, _tokenContract, _quantity);
426:     }
427: 
````

### The Issue
As you can see on line 413 above as part of unlock function, there is a forceHarvest called in contract accountManager. This is where the schnibbles are being harvested. 

See below the detail of _harvest function as part of forceHarvest. Let's focus on line 378-379. You will notice there is 1 days denominator which is equivalent to 86,400. If the numerator (dailySchnibbles * secondsToClaim) did not reached 86,400 , the result of harvestedSchnibbles will be zero. 

This could be a problem if the user decided to unlock his tokens in short period of time (few secondstoclaim) and at same time daily schnibble figure is also few in which if you multiply both figures is still not enough to reach 86,400.

````Solidity
File: AccountManager.sol
372:     function _harvest(address _caller) private returns (uint256 _harvested) {
373:         (uint256 dailySchnibbles, uint256 bonus) = getDailySchnibbles(_caller);
374:         dailySchnibbles += ((dailySchnibbles * bonus) / 1e18);
375: 
376:         uint256 secondsToClaim = block.timestamp -
377:             players[_caller].lastHarvestDate;
378:         uint256 harvestedSchnibbles = (dailySchnibbles * secondsToClaim) /
379:             1 days;
380: 
381:         players[_caller].unfedSchnibbles += harvestedSchnibbles;
382:         players[_caller].lastHarvestDate = uint32(block.timestamp);
383: 
384:         _harvested = harvestedSchnibbles;
385: 
386:         emit Harvested(_caller, harvestedSchnibbles);
387:     }
````



## Impact
Lost of harvested schnibbles

## Proof of Concept
Consider this scenario.
1. User A decided to lock this tokens to the contract within just a short period of time. Let's say 10,000 seconds. 
2. After 10,000 seconds, User A decided to unlock his tokens. Let's say the computed sample daily schnibble is only 5, we need to multiply it to 10,000 seconds. Why 10,000 seconds? because this is considered the secondsToClaim, difference between last harvest date (date of locking token) until the unlocking date.
3. The numerator is (5*10,000) = 50,000 and then divided by 86,400, the harvestedSchnibbles will be zero. 

````Solidity
376:         uint256 secondsToClaim = block.timestamp -
377:             players[_caller].lastHarvestDate;
378:         uint256 harvestedSchnibbles = (dailySchnibbles * secondsToClaim) /
379:             1 days;
````
## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a minimum lock duration of 86,400 or 1 day to function setLockDuration in order to be aligned with the formula of harvest function in account manager.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L374-L377


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `LockManager` contract's `_lock` function uses the `transferFrom` method to transfer tokens from a user's address to the contract. However, not all ERC20 tokens adhere to the standard of reverting on failure; some tokens, such as ZRX, return false instead of reverting. If the `transferFrom` function fails and returns false, but this return value is not checked, it can lead to tokens not being transferred as intended. This oversight can cause significant issues, such as inaccurate token balances, failure to lock tokens, and potential loss of funds or contract malfunction.

## Proof of Concept

In the `LockManager` contract, the `_lock` function contains the following code:

```solidity
if (_tokenContract != address(0)) {
    IERC20 token = IERC20(_tokenContract);
    token.transferFrom(_tokenOwner, address(this), _quantity);
}
```

If the `transferFrom` function fails (e.g., the token contract returns false), this failure will not be detected, and the function will proceed as if the tokens were successfully transferred.

### Example of Vulnerable Token

Some tokens, such as ZRX, do not revert on failure but instead return false. You can find more examples of such tokens in the [Weird ERC20 tokens list](https://github.com/d-xo/weird-erc20/#no-revert-on-failure).

## Tools Used

- Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To ensure safe token transfers, use the `safeTransferFrom` method provided by the OpenZeppelin `SafeERC20` library. This method handles non-standard ERC20 tokens that return false instead of reverting on failure.

Refactor the `_lock` function as follows:

1. Import the SafeERC20 library:

   ```solidity
   import "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol";
   ```

2. Use the `safeTransferFrom` method:
   ```solidity
   if (_tokenContract != address(0)) {
       IERC20 token = IERC20(_tokenContract);
       SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom(token, _tokenOwner, address(this), _quantity);
   }
   ```

This change ensures that the transfer will revert if it fails, thereby maintaining the contract's integrity and preventing potential issues arising from failed token transfers.

By implementing `safeTransferFrom`, you safeguard against the risks associated with tokens that do not revert on failure, ensuring that the `_lock` function operates as intended and only proceeds when tokens are successfully transferred.



## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L419-L423
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L376


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Impact is HIGH. This issue could potentially lead to loss of funds and can make a user unable to unlock their locked tokens.

## Proof of Concept

For the scope of this audit, the [README](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables#general-questions) states that we can assume more tokens can be added for use in `LockManager` in future.

|Question|	Answer|
|-|-|
|ERC20 used by the protocol	|USDB, WETH, (assume we can add more to the future for use in LockManager)|

[Also according to the README,](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables#erc20-token-behaviors-in-scope) 

ERC20 token behaviors in scope:
| Question| Answer|
|-|-|
|Doesn't revert on failure|	Yes|

In the `LockManager.sol` contract, the `transferFrom` and transfer function is used without checking its return value:

```solidity
IERC20 token = IERC20(_tokenContract);
token.transferFrom(_tokenOwner, address(this), _quantity);
```

```solidity
 // send token
        if (_tokenContract == address(0)) {
            payable(msg.sender).transfer(_quantity);
        } else {
            IERC20 token = IERC20(_tokenContract);
            token.transfer(msg.sender, _quantity);
        }
```


Now, `ZRX` is a token that fits these conditions and can theoretically be used in `LockManager` as a principal token. https://coinmarketcap.com/dexscan/ethereum/0xfa97aa5002124fe7edd36584628300e8d81df042/

ZRX is a token that does not revert on failure, instead it simply returns a bool value that is not checked.

If `_tokenContract` is a token that does not revert on failure, this call could fail silently, allowing the rest of the function to execute as if the transfer were successful.

Similarly, `BNB` just like ZRX does not revert on failure, instead it simply returns a bool value that is not checked too: https://etherscan.io/token/0xB8c77482e45F1F44dE1745F52C74426C631bDD52



Now in the current scope, Unsafe transfers are used in [_lock](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L376) and [unlock](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L420-L423) functions.

Since these attempts to transfer could silently fail, this then leads to multiple scenarios like:

- Loss of Funds: If a user attempts to lock tokens using a token that does not revert on failure, and the transferFrom operation fails silently, the user might still believe their tokens are successfully locked. Albeit, due to the lack of actual token transfer, the user's tokens would not be properly recorded in the contract's state. This could lead to the user losing access to their tokens indefinitely, as the contract would not recognize them as being locked.

- Incorrect Rewards Calculation: The LockManager contract [calculates rewards](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L341) based on the amount of tokens locked and the duration of the lock. If the token transfer fails but the contract proceeds as if it succeeded, the reward calculations could be skewed, resulting in users receiving less than what they are entitled to.

- Inability to Unlock Tokens: Since the contract relies on accurate tracking of locked tokens to facilitate unlocking, a failed transfer could mean that the contract's state does not reflect the user's intention to lock tokens. Consequently, the user might find themselves unable to unlock their tokens, effectively leading to loses.


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps:

Ensure that the return value of `transferFrom` is always checked, and the transaction is reverted if the transfer fails Or use openzeppelin's `SafeERC20`'s library 






## Assessed type

ERC20

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L142-L242


# Vulnerability details

# Vulnerability details

A stalemate can occur if 2 users approve and 2 users disapprove a proposal, making the contract ineffective as no new proposals can be made or resolved.

# Impact

- Unresolved Proposals: Proposals can remain unresolved indefinitely, making the contract ineffective.
- Contract Uselessness: No new proposals can be made, rendering the contract useless.
## Proof of Concept

Users with the `pricefeed_n` role can create a proposal. If 2 users approve and 2 users disapprove, the proposal remains unresolved because 2 votes are less than both the `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` and `DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD`. Since the same address cannot both approve and disapprove, the proposal cannot be dropped, leading to a deadlock. This makes the contract ineffective.

## Tool used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
**Possible Solutions**
1. Decrease the Threshold Number:
   - Lower the `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` and `DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD` to reduce the likelihood of a stalemate.
2. Increase the Number of Addresses:
   - Add another address to the voting pool, increasing the total number of voters to 6. This reduces the chance of a tie, as an even number of voters can prevent a stalemate situation.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L177
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L210


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
It's possible for an authorized caller to call disapproveUSDPrice and then call approveUSDPrice. This means an authorized caller can have disapproval and approval counts at the same time.

This can even lead to a situation where usd price can't be updated. For instance, if the number of authorized callers is 5. One user approves and disapproves a usd price, the four other callers approve and disapprove equally (2 for, 2 against).

With the initial user having an "approve" and "disapprove", "approve" would be 3 likewise "disapprove".

## Proof of Concept
An authorized caller can call disapproveUSDPrice funtion first. Then, call approveUSDPrice function after. 

Unlike in disapproveUSDPrice function, there's nothing stopping an authorized caller, who has called disappproveUSDPrice function initially, from calling approveUSDPrice function.

In essence, an authorized caller can have his "vote" count for approve usd price and disapprove usd price.



## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In approveUSDPrice function, also check if msg.seder has already called disapproveUSDPrice function.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L142
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L177
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L506


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
usdPriceProposal can be deleted without approval when approveUSDPrice is called and also without approveUSDPrice reverting.

## Proof of Concept
In prooposeUSDPrice(), it has a parameter called _contracts that accepts a list of addresses. However, these addresses are not checked that non is zero address is present. The only check in the function is _contracts.length is not zero.

`  if (_contracts.length == 0) revert ProposalInvalidContractsError();`

The length of the contract may not be zero but can include a zero address. For instance, if there are 5 contract addresses passed into the _contracts parameter, and one of the addresses is a zero address, this will pass the above check.

The check for zero address in _contracts parameter is also missing in approveUSDPrice() and _execUSDPriceUpdate().

Now in _execUSDPriceUpdate(), `delete usdUpdateProposal` is outside the for loop. What this means is when any of the addresses passed into _contracts parameter is zero in proposeUSDPrice() and approveUSDPrice() is called, which in turn calls the internal _execUSDPriceUpdate(), and gets to this line in _execUSDPriceUpdate():

` if (configuredTokens[tokenContract].nftCost != 0) {`

The for loop will be skipped when a zero address is passed as part of the _contracts parameter without reverting. And the code will proceed to still delete usdUpdateProposal without reverting and also without updating usd price.

Note that this vulnerability would still occur when APPROVE_THRESHOLD is met.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
There should be a check for address zero in proposeUSDPrice().
Also, delete usdUpdateProposal should be inside the for loop in _execUSDPriceUpdate(). 








## Assessed type

Access Control

raw_row.title: Incorrect unlockTime calculation when unlockTime is extended

title: Incorrect unlockTime calculation when unlockTime is extended
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L265-L267


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
unlockTime can be shortened when lock duration is extended

## Proof of Concept
The issue lies in the calculation of the new unlockTime for the locked tokens.

``
      uint32 lastLockTime = lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract]
                    .lastLockTime;
                lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
                    lastLockTime +
                    uint32(_duration);
            }

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L263C13-L268C14

The code assumes that the lastLockTime stored in the lockedTokens mapping represents the time when the tokens were last locked. However, it does not consider the possibility that the user may have set a different lock duration in the past, which could have already extended the unlockTime.

In this case, simply adding the new _duration to the lastLockTime would result in an incorrect unlockTime. 

Suppose a user, Alice, has locked some tokens for a duration of 30 days (2,592,000 seconds) on January 1st, 2023, at 12:00:00 UTC.
Initially, the lockedTokens mapping would be:

`lockedTokens[Alice][tokenContract] = {
    quantity: 1000,
    lastLockTime: 1672531200, // January 1st, 2023, 12:00:00 UTC
    unlockTime: 1675123200, // January 31st, 2023, 12:00:00 UTC (lastLockTime + 30 days)
    remainder: 0
}`

Now, let's say on January 15th, 2023, at 12:00:00 UTC, Alice wants to extend the lock duration to 45 days (3,888,000 seconds).
According to the current implementation, the code would calculate the new unlockTime as follows:

`uint32 lastLockTime = lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].lastLockTime; // 1672531200
lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
    lastLockTime +
    uint32(_duration); // 1672531200 + 3888000 = 1676419200`

The new unlockTime would be set to 1676419200, which corresponds to February 14th, 2023, 12:00:00 UTC.

However, this calculation is incorrect because it does not consider the original unlockTime of January 31st, 2023, 12:00:00 UTC. The correct unlockTime should be calculated based on the current block.timestamp (January 15th, 2023, 12:00:00 UTC) plus the new lock duration of 45 days.

The correct unlockTime should be 1677654000, which corresponds to March 1st, 2023, 12:00:00 UTC, as expected.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The new unlockTime should be calculated based on the current block.timestamp and the new _duration.

`lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
    uint32(block.timestamp) +
    uint32(_duration);`


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L275-L294

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A malicious user can call the lockOnBehalf function with a valid _onBehalfOf address and a _quantity of zero, effectively extending the lock duration of the _onBehalfOf address without actually locking any tokens.

## Proof of Concept
The lockOnBehalf function allows a user to lock tokens on behalf of another address (_onBehalfOf). However, the function does not check if the _quantity parameter is greater than zero. 

This allows a malicious user to pass a valid _onBehalfOf address and a _quantity of zero, effectively extending the lock duration of the _onBehalfOf address without actually locking any tokens.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In the lockOnBehalf function, add a check to ensure that the _quantity parameter is greater than zero before calling the _lock function. This will prevent the lock duration from being extended without actually locking any tokens.

`if (_quantity == 0) revert ZeroQuantityError();`

raw_row.title: Players Who Lock Value Less Than the NFT Cost Won't Receive Any NFT during the lock period

title: Players Who Lock Value Less Than the NFT Cost Won't Receive Any NFT during the lock period
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L363-L364
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L379


# Vulnerability details

If a player locks a value less than the `nftCost`, they will not receive any NFTs because the amount they have locked is insufficient to meet the minimum requirement for one NFT. Instead, the entire locked amount will be treated as a remainder, which will be stored in the player's `lockedToken.remainder`. even when` lockPeriod ` have not ended. This is displeasing as every lock should result in at least one NFT.
The `nftCost` can't be known to players as there no the `getNftCost` function users will have to guess the amount.

## Impact
Without knowing the correct `nftCost` users are forced to lock any amount.
Players who deposit an amount less than the NFT cost will not receive any NFTs because their locked funds are insufficient to cover the cost of one NFT. This will lead  to displeasure among users, as their locked funds are stored as a remainder, which might not be immediately clear or useful unless additional funds are deposited later to meet the NFT cost. Assuming they can afford it.

## Proof of Concept
When a player locks funds that are less than the `nftCost`, the calculation logic results in the entire amount being treated as a remainder, and no NFTs are awarded.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L363-L364 
```solidity
                // calculate number of nfts
                remainder = quantity % configuredToken.nftCost;
                numberNFTs = (quantity - remainder) / configuredToken.nftCost;
```


Example Scenario:
- Suppose the `nftCost` is 1.5 ETH.
- A player locks 1 ETH, which is less than the `nftCost`.

The calculation will be:

```solidity
uint256 remainder = 1 % 1.5; // remainder = 1
uint256 numberNFTs = (1 - 1) / 1.5; // numberNFTs = 0
```
In this case, the `remainder` is 5 ETH, and `numberNFTs` is 0.

The remainder of 1 ETH is stored in the player's `lockedToken.remainder`:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L379
```solidity
lockedToken.remainder = remainder;
lockedToken.quantity += _quantity;
lockedToken.lastLockTime = uint32(block.timestamp);
lockedToken.unlockTime = uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_lockDuration);
```
Since the amount locked is less than the `nftCost`, no NFTs are issued, and the entire amount is simply stored as a remainder.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
 Consider setting a minimum lock amount that is equal to or greater than the `nftCost` to prevent users from locking insufficient amounts. This ensures that every lock results in at least one NFT being awarded.
Include a `getNftCost` function.





## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L297
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L89-L95


# Vulnerability details

The `lockdrop` contract allows users to lock their asset for a certain period of time while they receive NFTS and Bonuses for doing so. This is fine if users only interact with the UX but if users interact directly with the contract and they send their assets directly into the contract whether the `lockPeriod` is active or not the assets will be lost forever as there's no mechanism in place to retrieve assets sent directly into the contract. 
## Impact
Players who interact with smart contracts directly on the Blockchain might send assets directly into the `lockdrop` without calling the `lock` function as there's no mechanism to retrieve such deposits the assets will remain locked in the contract.

## Proof Of Concept
The required method to use the `lockdrop` is by calling the `lock` function in the contract 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L297
```solidity
   function lock(
        address _tokenContract,
        uint256 _quantity
    )
        external
        payable
        notPaused
        onlyActiveToken(_tokenContract)
        onlyConfiguredToken(_tokenContract)
        nonReentrant
    {
        _lock(_tokenContract, _quantity, msg.sender, msg.sender);
    }
```
This locks the assets accordingly.
However users can mistakenly or knowingly send assets into the contract, sending ETH will revert due to the `fallback` and `receive` reverting when such happens 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L89-L95
```solidity
fallback() external payable {
        revert LockManagerInvalidCallError();
    }

    receive() external payable {
        revert LockManagerRefuseETHError();
    }
```
But if users send ERC20  tokens the tokens remain locked as there's no way to recover them .

## Tool Use
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Include a recovery logic for such mishaps

ERC20
