https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L380
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L401


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users will withdraw wrong amount of tokens (unlocking more/less than deserved) and danger of DOS is present for the last couple of people who try to unlock.

## Proof of Concept
Rebasing tokens (USDB) change their underlying balance based on certain condition. Balances can increase/decrease. The problem arises when we do a lock and we write in storage the amount of tokens that were transferred.

Code reference: [`link`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L380)

```solidity
  lockedToken.quantity += _quantity;
```

After some time this amount can change and the contract will hold more or less tokens but the value in storage (quantity) will not change.

Based on the direction of the change users will either:
1. Claim more tokens than deserved (if the token balance decreases due to a rebase) and the last users who wish to [`unlock()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L401) will not be able because there won't be enough tokens remaining in the contract
2. Claim less tokens, causing tokens to be locked in the contract - if the token balance increases.

Code reference: [`link`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L401-L427)
```solidity
function unlock(
    address _tokenContract,
    uint256 _quantity
) external notPaused nonReentrant {
    LockedToken storage lockedToken = lockedTokens[msg.sender][_tokenContract];
    ...
    lockedToken.quantity -= _quantity;
    ...
}
```

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider implementing a system to handle rebasing tokens. The simplest solution I can think of is to convert the rebasing token to their wrapped version. This way the current accounting will work. In the case of USDB, the tokens should be converted to nrUSDB.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L261


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The way lock duration is set by calling `LockManager::setLockDuration()` it is possible to set a lock duration which is less than minimum lock duration.
## Proof of Concept

Suppose minimum lock duration is 60 seconds. A lock was created at timestamp X which is the lastLockTime of the lock. So unlockTime will be (X + 60 seconds). 
```solidity
  lastLockTime(X)                                                unlockTime(X+60)
      |-------------------------------------------------------------|
       <------------- duration = minDuration = 60 secs ------------->
```
Now, at the time of (x+40 secs) player called the `setLockDuration()` with 30 secs as argument. As (X + 40 + 30) = (x + 70) is greater than the unlockTime i.e (X+60) so the call will not revert by `LockDurationReducedError`. 
Finally unlockTime  = lastLockTime + duration = X + 30.
As of the new unlockTime the lock is already unlocked.
So we can see that actually (X + 30) is far less than minimum duration, still the player managed to unlock 20 seconds before [because he called the `setLockDuration()` at (X + 40).
The problem is in the process of checking the condition for whether the duration is reduced or not i.e `LockDurationReducedError`. The `if` condition looks like:
```solidity
                if (
                    uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) <
                    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
                ) {
                    revert LockDurationReducedError();
                }
```
You can see that `uint32(_duration)` is added with block.timestamp but it should not, it should be added with `lastLockTime`.
The new duration looks like:
```solidity
                                           X + 40 secs
  lastLockTime(X)                      setLockDuration()         unlockTime(X+60)
      |--------------------------------------|-----------------------|
       <------------- duration = minDuration = 60 secs ------------->

      X                            X+30
      |-----------------------------|
      <----- new duration = 30 ----->
```


## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change the `if` block from present to this:
```solidity
                if (
                    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].lastLockTime + uint32(_duration) <
                    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
                ) {
                    revert LockDurationReducedError();
                }
```


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L177-L207
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L210-L242


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In current implementation, both `approveUSDPrice` and `disapproveUSDPrice` are allowed to be called for the same one proposal. 
For `approveUSDPrice`, if `usdUpdateProposal.approvalsCount >= APPROVE_THRESHOLD` is met, `_execUSDPriceUpdate` will be called to [update the price](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L202-L204).
On the other hand, for `disapproveUSDPrice`, if `usdUpdateProposal.disapprovalsCount >= DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD` is met, the proposal will [be deleted](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L237-L241)

## Proof of Concept
There is an extreme case that those two functions might not work as expected.
Suppose both `usdUpdateProposal.approvalsCount` and `usdUpdateProposal.disapprovalsCount` are 3

1. Role.PriceFeed_1 calls `proposeUSDPrice` to create a proposal, and Role.PriceFeed_2 calls `approveUSDPrice` to approve the proposal
2. Role.PriceFeed_3 and Role.PriceFeed_4 calls `disapproveUSDPrice`
3. now both `usdUpdateProposal.approvalsCount` and `usdUpdateProposal.disapprovalsCount` are 2
4. Role.PriceFeed_5 calls `approveUSDPrice` to approve the proposal, but later it calls `disapproveUSDPrice` to disapprove the **same** proposal
5. If everything works as expected, Role.PriceFeed_5's `approveUSDPrice` will be executed first, and [_execUSDPriceUpdate](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L202-L204) will be executed.
6. But if the re-org happens, `disapproveUSDPrice` will be executed first, and the proposal [will be cleared](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L237-L241)

# Vulnerability details

Quoting from [Attack ideas (where to focus for bugs)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/tree/main?tab=readme-ov-file#attack-ideas-where-to-focus-for-bugs):
>and that people cannot reduce lockup times that are previously set.

It means that `lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime` can't be reduced.
But according to the implementation, `lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime` can be reduced.

## Proof of Concept
In [LockManager.sol#L256-L261](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L261), the function use `uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime` to make sure that `unlockTime` can't be reduced, but this is not correct.

Suppose current `block.timestamp` is 1716634739(Sat May 25 18:58:59 CST 2024)
before calling `setLockDuration`:
`lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime` is 1718362739(Fri Jun 14 18:58:59 CST 2024)
`lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].lastLockTime` is 1715770739(Wed May 15 18:58:59 CST 2024)

If we call `setLockDuration` using 20 days as parameter:
The check in [LockManager.sol#L256-L261](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L261) will be passed because:
1716634739 + 21 days == 1718362739 == lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime

And then in [LockManager.sol#L265-L267](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L265-L267), the `lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime` will be 1715770739 + 20 days == 1717498739, which is Tue Jun  4 18:58:59 CST 2024.

So `and that people cannot reduce lockup times that are previously set.` is broken.

But [lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L258C21-L258C71) can be updated by [_unlock](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L382-L384), and `_unlock` can be called by `lockOnBehalf` and `lock`.

So when after a normal calls `lock` or a malicious user calls `lockOnBehalf`, the value of `_duration` will restricted. Only the value that pass the [if condition](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L261) can be set.

## Proof of Concept
Supposed Alice(the normal user) hasn't locked any assets in the contract, she call call `setLockDuration` with __any value__ as `_duration` as long as the value is not greater than `configStorage.getUint(StorageKey.MaxLockDuration)` in [LockManager.sol#L246-L247](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L246-L247).

But before Alice's call, Bob(the malicious user) calls `lockOnBehalf` with __1 wei__ as _quantity, and Alice's address as `_onBehalfOf`.

Then in [LockManager.sol#L382-L384](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L382-L384), `lockedToken.unlockTime` will be set.

So when Alice's tx is executed, only the `_duration` that can pass the [if check](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L261) can be updated.

__Besides Bob can be DOSed by other user, he might be DOSed by himself after calling `lock`__

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L260
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L266


# Vulnerability details

## Description
The setLockDuration function does a couple of checks to ensure the new lock duration does not decrease the previously existing one. However, its current logic allows this requirement to be bypassed.
This happens due to the following reasons: 
The function does not check if the uint256 duration argument is smaller than the minimum duration at the contract.

The LockDurationReducedError only checks for the current timestamp + duration in comparision to the last unlockTime:
```solidity
 if (
                    uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) <
                    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
                ) {
                    revert LockDurationReducedError();
                }

```

The new unlockTime is not based on the previously used, but on the lastLockTime - that is, the time the previous lock was created.
```solidity
uint32 lastLockTime = lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract]
                    .lastLockTime;
                lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
                    lastLockTime +
                    uint32(_duration);
```

This enables malicious parties to reduce the lock duration by doing the following steps:
1. Create a lock. Say the lock starts at timestamp 1000 and it has a duration of 1000 seconds. This lock will have a lastLockTime of 1000 and unlockTime of 2000.
2. Wait 500 seconds. Call setLockDuration with the new duration as 501 seconds.
	1. The call will not revert as the LockDurationReducedError won't be executed: the current block.timestamp + the new duration results in a timestamp that is equal to 2001, bigger than the unlockTime (2000).
	2. Unlock time will become lastLockTime + new duration. Since lastLockTime is 1000, the new unlockTime is 1501.
3. Wait 1 second. Call unlock and recover the funds after almost half of the lock's duration.
Notice: lock durations and timestamps here provided are for the purpose of exemplifying and the logic does apply to different values.
## Impact
Locks are able to be manipulated to last half of its original duration.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Make sure to review the LockDurationReducedError checks.
If the intention is to never allow lock duration reductions, the check should evaluate duration + last lock time instead of block.timestamp + duration, as can be seen in the code snippet bellow:
```solidity
 if (
                    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract]
                    .lastLockTime + uint32(_duration) <
                    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
                ) {
                    revert LockDurationReducedError();
                }
```

This will ensure the new unlock time fits the bounds defined by the initial lock timestamp.


## Assessed type

Timing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L275


# Vulnerability details

## Description
The lock private function increases the amount of certain token locked by an address at the LockManager contract by transferring a corresponding amount of tokens into it.
As a side-effect, it increases the unlockTime by the current lock's lock duration.
This opens up the possibility of attackers to lock someone's tokens forever at the contract.

The reason for that is the lock private function has two entry points: via the lock and via the lockOnBehalf functions. The latter allows anyone to target any address as the tokenRecipient - as it offers no access control from callers to lock recipients.
If any address can be targeted, anyone can increase a lock's unlock time, as can be seen in the following code snippet:
```solidity

function _lock(
        address _tokenContract,
        uint256 _quantity,
        address _tokenOwner,
        address _lockRecipient
    ) private {
...		
		lockedToken.unlockTime =
            uint32(block.timestamp) +
            uint32(_lockDuration);
...
}
```
## Impact
Malicious actors can freely increase the unlock time of users' locks.
If the gas cost is low at any point, then maintaining one's lock forever is relatively cheap.
## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Make sure to create some sort of access control for locking on behalf of someone, as it has the side-effect of increasing the unlock time. 
An interesting possibility would be to create a mapping of allowed addresses to lock on behalf of an address then check if the lock on behalf caller is allowed to do such an action to its lock recipient.
This access control logic will mitigate the aforementioned attack vector.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L353
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L379


# Vulnerability details

## Description
The lock private function can be executed from the lock and from the lockOnBehalf public functions.
When called in periods outside of lock drops, the lock private function does a wrong state management on a locked token's remainder.
Let's analyze it in-depth:
The remainder uint256 variable is initialized as equal to zero:
```solidity
uint256 remainder;
```

Then the function proceeds to update this variable only if the current block timestamp is within the lockdrop bounds:
```solidity
if (
            lockdrop.start <= uint32(block.timestamp) &&
            lockdrop.end >= uint32(block.timestamp)
        ) {
...
remainder = quantity % configuredToken.nftCost;
...
}
```

Finally it takes the current remainder value and updates the remainder at the lockedToken storage mapping:
```solidity
lockedToken.remainder = remainder;
```

The issue with that is that if we don't ever reach the if block limited by the lock drop start and end, we put a zero-valued remainder at the storage in lockedToken.remainder. This removes any remainder the user had left.
## Impact
Users that call lock outside of the lockdrop period will lose the remainders accumulated on previous deposits
## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Make sure to avoid updating the remainder storage variable inside a lockedToken if the currently calculated value is not different than the previously held. An interesting way would to keep the remainder value would be through an else block:
```solidity
if (
            lockdrop.start <= uint32(block.timestamp) &&
            lockdrop.end >= uint32(block.timestamp)
        ) {
...
}
else {
	remainder = lockedToken.remainder;
}
```

This should suffice to ensure the remainder is not lost in such cases.


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L194
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L227


# Vulnerability details

## Description
When dealing with usd price proposals, price feeds ought to have two options:
vote to approve or to disapprove a proposed price.
This is not enforced on its entirety at the LockManager contract, however.
The disapproveUSDPrice function properly enforces that by checking whether the price feed hasn't approved nor disapproved a proposed price before accounting the disapprove vote:
```solidity
function disapproveUSDPrice(
        uint256 _price
    )
    ...
    if (usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
            revert ProposalAlreadyApprovedError();
        if (usdUpdateProposal.disapprovals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
            revert ProposalAlreadyDisapprovedError();
            ...
```

The approveUSDPrice doesn't enforce the same checks. It only verifies the price feed hasn't approved the price priorly:
```solidity
function approveUSDPrice(
        uint256 _price
    )
    ...
    if (usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
            revert ProposalAlreadyApprovedError();
    ...
```
## Impact
The current price approval mechanism is not fair on all price fees.
This issue allows privilege escalation as a price feed is able to vote twice.

Allowing one voter to vote on both approval and disapproval exceeds the intended permissions by creating the possibility of voting ties: the system has 5 price feeds so that ties are impossible, but this privilege escalation allows both for and against positions to have 3 or more votes. This enables an unexpected logic for price approvals - price feeds will have incentives to vote as soon as possible.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add the following check to approveUSDPrice:
```solidity
        if (usdUpdateProposal.disapprovals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
            revert ProposalAlreadyDisapprovedError();
```


## Assessed type

Other

## Proof of Concept
1. Bob creates a lock and increased duration to maxDuration.
2. Bob is 5mins away from unlocking funds.
3. Alice calls ```lockOnBehalf()``` with one Wei and Bod address as the ```lockRecipient```

```solidity
    function lockOnBehalf(
        address _tokenContract,
        uint256 _quantity,
        address _onBehalfOf
    )
        external
        payable
        notPaused
        onlyActiveToken(_tokenContract)
        onlyConfiguredToken(_tokenContract)
        nonReentrant
    {
        address tokenOwner = msg.sender;
        address lockRecipient = msg.sender;
        if (_onBehalfOf != address(0)) {
            lockRecipient = _onBehalfOf;
        }

        _lock(_tokenContract, _quantity, tokenOwner, lockRecipient);
    }
```
4. Bob lockDuration is looked up and ```unlockTime``` is extended with ```lockDuration``` to start another cycle.
```solidity
...
 uint32 _lockDuration = playerSettings[_lockRecipient].lockDuration;
...
 lockedToken.unlockTime =
            uint32(block.timestamp) +
            uint32(_lockDuration);
```

## Tools Used
Manual review. 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Map locks to different unlockTime.
1. User token locks should be an array.
2. ArrayIndex should then be mapped to unLockTime.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L245-L249


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When setting new lock duration, `setLockDuration` does not check the lower limit of the duration, thus the new duration can be smaller than the minimum duration (i.e. `lockdrop.minLockDuration`), breaking the minimum lock duration limitation of the contract.

## Proof of Concept
According to function `_lock`, the lock duration should be greater than `lockdrop.minLockDuration` and less than `configStorage.getUint(StorageKey.MaxLockDuration)` (L350, L357), otherwise the lock tx reverts.
```solidity
Function: _lock

349:        if (_lockDuration == 0) {
350:@>          _lockDuration = lockdrop.minLockDuration;
351:        }
352:        if (
353:            lockdrop.start <= uint32(block.timestamp) &&
354:            lockdrop.end >= uint32(block.timestamp)
355:        ) {
356:            if (
357:@>              _lockDuration < lockdrop.minLockDuration ||
358:                _lockDuration >
359:                uint32(configStorage.getUint(StorageKey.MaxLockDuration))
360:            ) revert InvalidLockDurationError();
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L349-L360

However, `setLockDuration` function only compare the new lock duration to the maximum duration (i.e. `configStorage.getUint(StorageKey.MaxLockDuration)`), not to the minimum (i.e. `lockdrop.minLockDuration`). So the new duration is possible to be smaller than `lockdrop.minLockDuration`, which breaks the minimum lock duration limitation of the contract.
```solidity
245:    function setLockDuration(uint256 _duration) external notPaused {
246:@>      if (_duration > configStorage.getUint(StorageKey.MaxLockDuration))
247:            revert MaximumLockDurationError();
248:
249:        playerSettings[msg.sender].lockDuration = uint32(_duration);
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L245-L249

## Tools Used
VS Code

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Revert the tx if `_duration < lockdrop.minLockDuration` at the begining of function `setLockDuration`.
```solidity
    function setLockDuration(uint256 _duration) external notPaused {
        if (_duration > configStorage.getUint(StorageKey.MaxLockDuration))
            revert MaximumLockDurationError();
+       if (_duration < lockdrop.minLockDuration)
+           revert MinimumLockDurationError();
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L177-L200


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
An oracle can approve an USD price even if it has disapproved the price already.

## Proof of Concept
When an oracle approves an USD price, function `approveUSDPrice` only check if the oracle has *approved* the price already, and reverts the tx if it has. But the function does not check if the oracle has *disapproved* the price already. As a result, the oracle can first disapprove the price, and then approve the price again. This may mess up the pricing of tokens.
```solidity
177:    function approveUSDPrice(
178:        uint256 _price
179:    )
180:        external
181:        onlyOneOfRoles(
182:            [
183:                Role.PriceFeed_1,
184:                Role.PriceFeed_2,
185:                Role.PriceFeed_3,
186:                Role.PriceFeed_4,
187:                Role.PriceFeed_5
188:            ]
189:        )
190:    {
191:        if (usdUpdateProposal.proposer == address(0)) revert NoProposalError();
192:        if (usdUpdateProposal.proposer == msg.sender)
193:            revert ProposerCannotApproveError();
194:@>      if (usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
195:            revert ProposalAlreadyApprovedError();
196:        if (usdUpdateProposal.proposedPrice != _price)
197:            revert ProposalPriceNotMatchedError();
198:
199:        usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender] = _usdProposalId;
200:        usdUpdateProposal.approvalsCount++;
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L177-L200

## Tools Used
VS Code

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In function `approveUSDPrice`, check if the oracle has disapproved the USD price, and revert the tx if it has.

        uint256 _price
    )
        ...
    {
        ...
        if (usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
            revert ProposalAlreadyApprovedError();
+       if (usdUpdateProposal.disapprovals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
+           revert ProposalAlreadyDisapprovedError();
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L16-L18


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

According to provided [documentation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/guides/CONSTANTS.md), roles:
* `PriceFeed_1`
* `PriceFeed_2`
* `PriceFeed_3`
* `PriceFeed_4`
* `PriceFeed_5`

are the addresses allowed to propose and vote on USD price updates. This implies, that there are 5 different roles (`PriceFeed_1` - `PriceFeed_5`) which can propose USD price and/or vote for that proposal.
Each role can contain multiple of addresses (to confirm that, please take a look at `setRole()` function from `ConfigStorage.sol` - a single role can be assigned to multiple of addresses).
This (having 5 roles, each containing multiple of addresses), allows us to assume, that there might be a lot of addresses which can vote for the proposal.

However, the protocol implements `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` and `DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD` as `uint8`, which basically means, that the max threshold for executing or removing a proposal is 255 (`type(uint8).max`). This obviously is not enough when there are many voters.

Moreover, please notice, that according to provided documentation, I treat (`PriceFeed_1` - `PriceFeed_5`) as non-trusted roles, because the protocol explicitly mentions that no roles are trusted:

[File: README.md](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/README.md#all-trusted-roles-in-the-protocol)
```
All trusted roles in the protocol

N/A
```


## Proof of Concept

Function `approveUSDPrice()` (which allows to vote for the proposal) and function `disapproveUSDPrice()` (which allows to vote against the proposal) implements `onlyOneOfToles()` modifier:

```
        onlyOneOfRoles(
            [
                Role.PriceFeed_1,
                Role.PriceFeed_2,
                Role.PriceFeed_3,
                Role.PriceFeed_4,
                Role.PriceFeed_5
            ]
        )
```

This modifier basically states, that any address which belongs to role `Role.PriceFeed_1`, `Role.PriceFeed_2`, `Role.PriceFeed_3`, `Role.PriceFeed_4`, `Role.PriceFeed_5` can vote for (or against) the proposal.

As 5 roles (each of those role can contain multiple of addresses) can vote for/against the proposal - we should assume that voting is designed for a significantly big number of users.

Each voting is bound by previously defined threshold (if there are more "yes" votes than the defined threshold, the proposal will be executed):

[File: LockManager.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L506-L509)
```
    function _execUSDPriceUpdate() internal {
        if (
            usdUpdateProposal.approvalsCount >= APPROVE_THRESHOLD &&
            usdUpdateProposal.disapprovalsCount < DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD
```
However, the `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` and `DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD` are defined as `uint8`:

[File: LockManager](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L16-L18C)
```
    uint8 APPROVE_THRESHOLD = 3;
    /// @notice Threshold for removing a proposal
    uint8 DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD = 3;
```

This means, that the maximum `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` could be 255. This limit might not be enough when there are multiple of voters.

Having multiple of roles which allows to vote for the proposal implies, that protocol expects a lot of users taking part in the voting. The more voters available to vote, the bigger threshold should be. E.g., the default value of `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` is set to `3`. For the scenario, that there are only 5 users who are able to vote, this threshold states that more than half of eligible to vote users need to approve the proposal. However, this threshold becomes negligible when the number of users who can vote is being significantly increased.

E.g., let's assume that there are 1500 users who can vote. The maximum threshold for accepting the proposal is 255, thus it's less than 20% users which can accept the proposal (255/1500 = 0.17) - and it's not possible to increase the threshold.

Because the maximum value of `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` is 255, the maximum threshold to approve the proposal is defined as below:

```
255 / (numberOfUsersWithRole(Role.PriceFeed_1) + numberOfUsersWithRole(Role.PriceFeed_2) + numberOfUsersWithRole(Role.PriceFeed_3) + numberOfUsersWithRole(Role.PriceFeed_4) + numberOfUsersWithRole(Role.PriceFeed_5))
```

When there are a lot of users who can vote - it won't be possible to set a proper threshold. This put the whole voting for a proposal at risk - even for the maximum threshold, only 255 votes would be enough to accept any proposal.



## Tools Used

Manual code review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Define `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` and `DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD` as `uint256` (or `uint32` at least). This would allow to set higher thresholds when protocol will have more users in `Role.PriceFeed_1`, `Role.PriceFeed_2`, `Role.PriceFeed_3`, `Role.PriceFeed_4`, `Role.PriceFeed_5` roles.






## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L129-L135


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

According to provided documentation, protocol does not implement any trusted role, which implicitly implies, that every role within the protocol should be treated as a non-trusted:

[File: README.md](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/README.md#all-trusted-roles-in-the-protocol)
```
All trusted roles in the protocol

N/A
```

Moreover, please notice, that each role might contain multiple of addresses (to confirm that, please take a look at `setRole()` function from `ConfigStorage.sol` - a single role can be assigned to multiple of addresses).


In the current attack scenario, we assume, that roles ` Role.PriceFeed_1` -  `Role.PriceFeed_5` can effectively block admin from changing the thresholds for executing proposal, by front-running every call to `setUSDThresholds()`.

Because thresholds can be changed only when there's no active proposal - malicious user can front-run `setUSDThresholds()` and set their own new proposals. This will block admin from changing the current proposal thresholds.

In some scenario, it's possible to completely break down the smart contract's functionality:

A). When some `Role.PriceFeed_1` -  `Role.PriceFeed_5` roles are being revoked, admin might decide to decrease the threshold. E.g., let's consider below scenario:

1) There are 6 users with roles `Role.PriceFeed_1` -  `Role.PriceFeed_5` (6 users can vote).
2) Both `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` and `DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD` is set to 4. This basically means that 4 of 6 users need to approve or disapprove the proposal. This is very reasonable settings, since more than 50% decide if the proposal would be executed or disapproved.
3) Admin decides to revoke 3 users from `Role.PriceFeed_1` -  `Role.PriceFeed_5`. This basically means, that there are only 3 users left who can vote on the proposal, but the threshold is set to 4 (thus it's unreachable - there are only 3 users who can vote and we need 4 votes to either approve or disapprove a proposal).
4) To fix this issue, admin needs to decrease the threshold. Admin decides to call `setUSDThresholds()` and decrease the threshold to 2.
5) One of the user front-runs `setUSDThresholds()` and calls `proposeUSDPrice()`.
6) New proposal is being created - that proposal still contains old threshold (4).
7) Because of the front-run, `setUSDThresholds()` reverts (when there's an active proposal, we cannot change the threshold, thus revert occurs).
8) Since new proposal is active, it's not possible to change the threshold unless that proposal becomes either executed or disapproved.
9) However, the proposal will never reach executed or disapproved state, because it requires 4 votes, where there are only 3 voters!
10) Contract is blocked, it's not possible to change the threshold and it's not possible to create any new proposal (only one proposal can be active). And because this proposal will never be either accepted or rejected - contract is blocked forever.


Additionally, the impact of this issue is significantly high when the thresholds are low and admin decides to increase them. There are multiple of scenarios when this issue might occur:

A). New users are being added to roles `Role.PriceFeed_1` -  `Role.PriceFeed_5`. Since there are more users who are able to vote for the proposal - the threshold should be increased. However, a single user can front-run `setUSDThresholds()` and create new proposal which will be using old `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` value. Since there are more users who can vote, reaching that threshold is being more possible.

B). The initial thresholds are set to very low values:

```
    uint8 APPROVE_THRESHOLD = 3;
    /// @notice Threshold for removing a proposal
    uint8 DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD = 3;
```

After contract deployment, admin might need to change these values to a higher values (especially, if there are many users with `Role.PriceFeed_1` -  `Role.PriceFeed_5` roles). However, a single user can effectively block changing those values by front-running `setUSDThresholds()` call.





## Proof of Concept

Setting thresholds (calling `setUSDThresholds()`) is only possible, when there's no active proposal in progress:

[File: LockManager.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L129-L135)
```
    function setUSDThresholds(
        uint8 _approve,
        uint8 _disapprove
    ) external onlyAdmin {
        if (usdUpdateProposal.proposer != address(0))
            revert ProposalInProgressError();
        APPROVE_THRESHOLD = _approve;
```

This implies, that the admin can change the threshold only when the previous proposal had been either approved or disapproved and no new proposal has been proposed.

This opens the door for front-running attacks. A malicious user, scans the mem-pool and sees that admin wants to update `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` by calling `setUSDThresholds()`. Then, the user immediately front-runs that call with `proposeUSDPrice()` function:

```
1. Admin wants to change the threshold, thus he calls setUSDThresholds()
2. User notices setUSDThresholds() call in the mem-pool and front-runs it with proposedUSDPrice()
3. proposedUSDPrice() is being called first, thus new proposal becomes active (usdUpdateProposal.proposer does not point to address(0) anymore).
4. Now, front-runned setUSDThresholds() is being executed, however, since there's an active proposal, setUSDThresholds() reverts at line 133)
5. The thresholds were not changed.
```


## Tools Used

Manual code review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Allow to change the threshold of the active proposal.



## Assessed type

MEV

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L142-L169


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

According to provided documentation, protocol does not implement any trusted role, which implicitly implies, that every role within the protocol should be treated as a non-trusted:

[File: README.md](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/README.md#all-trusted-roles-in-the-protocol)
```
All trusted roles in the protocol

N/A
```

In the current attack scenario, we assume, that roles `Role.PriceFeed_1` -  `Role.PriceFeed_5` can create a malicious proposal which will break down the whole protocol.

User can create a proposal which won't be executed (it will always revert during the execution). Since it's not possible to create multiple proposal at once - contract won't work at all!


## Proof of Concept

1. Create a malicious proposal, which contains multiple of addresses in `_contracts` array

[Fie: Lock.Manager.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L142-L144)
```
    function proposeUSDPrice(
        uint256 _price,
        address[] calldata _contracts
    )
        external
        onlyOneOfRoles(
     [...]
     usdUpdateProposal.contracts = _contracts;
```

E.g., `proposeUSDPrice(2, [0x01, 0x02, ...])`.
Calling above function means, that there will be a lot of addresses in `usdUpdateProposal.contracts`.

2. Now other users vote for or against that proposal. Let's assume the default scenario. There are 5 roles `Role.PriceFeed_1` -  `Role.PriceFeed_5` who can vote, thus for the simplicity, let's assume that there are only 5 voters.
The default thresholds values are:
```
    uint8 APPROVE_THRESHOLD = 3;
    /// @notice Threshold for removing a proposal
    uint8 DISAPPROVE_THRESHOLD = 3;
```

This means that they need to be either 3 `yes` votes to execute the proposal or 3 `no` votes to disapprove the proposal.
Let's assume that 3 users voted for `yes` and proposal can be executed.

3. Since proposal can be executed, we will be calling `_execUSDPriceUpdate()`

Let's notice, that function `_execUSDPriceUpdate()` loops over unbounded array.

[File: LockManager.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L511-L512)
```
            uint256 updateTokensLength = usdUpdateProposal.contracts.length;
            for (uint256 i; i < updateTokensLength; i++) {
```

This array contains multiple of addresses which were added via `proposeUSDPrice()` call. Because this array is so big, `execUSDPriceUpdate()` reverts with out of gas error.
It's not possible to execute the proposal - thus it will always revert with out of gas error.
It's not possible to reject the proposal either, because 3 of 5 users voted `yes`. This means that there are only 2 users who voted `no` - thus disapprove threshold is not being reached.

Moreover, it's not possible to change the threshold when the proposal is still active.
Moreover, it's not possible to propose any other proposal when one is still active.

This basically means, that protocol becomes broken down. There's one proposal which stuck the whole protocol.
We cannot execute it (it will revert with out of gas error). We cannot propose any new proposal (the old one needs to be either executed or rejected) and we cannot reject it (because the disapprove threshold cannot be met). Contract is blocked forever - no other proposal cannot be proposed - and the proposed one cannot be executed (or rejected).



## Tools Used

Manual code review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

According to provided [documentation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/README.md#erc20-token-behaviors-in-scope), protocol accepts ERC-20 tokens with high decimals:

```
ERC20 token behaviors in scope
[...]
Low decimals ( < 6)	Yes
High decimals ( > 18)	Yes
```

However, the code-base does not respect the documentation and does not work properly with tokens with high decimals.

Tokens with more than 18 decimals are not supported by the protocol (even though, the documentation explicitly states that protocol supports them). Function `getLockedWeightedValue()` will revert with underflow when ERC-20 tokens will have more than 18 decimals.

## Proof of Concept

[File: LockManager.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L472-L482)

                // We are assuming all tokens have a maximum of 18 decimals and that USD Price is denoted in 1e18
                uint256 deltaDecimal = 10 **
                    (18 -
                        configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals);
                lockedWeighted +=
                    (deltaDecimal *
                        lockedTokens[_player][configuredTokenContracts[i]]
                            .quantity *
                        configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]]
                            .usdPrice) /
                    1e18;
```

The comment at line 472 states that: `We are assuming all tokens have a maximum of 18 decimals and that USD Price is denoted in 1e18`. However, this assumption is wrong, because the documentation straightforwardly states that ERC-20 with high decimals (> 18) are in scope.

When provided ERC-20 have more than 18 decimals, the expression `(18 - configuredTokens[configuredTokenContracts[i]].decimals)` will underflow and revert.
This implies, that tokens with more than 18 decimals (e.g. YAM-V2 token has 24 decimal) won't work with the protocol.


## Tools Used

Manual code review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Do not assume that all tokens have a maximum of 18 decimals - because the documentation straightforwardly states that's not true. According to documentation, protocol should support tokens with both low ( < 6) and high ( > 18) decimals.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L461-L487


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In getLockedWeightedValue() we are calculating the USD value of all tokens locked by a player, weighted by their yield. if we have locked a token with 6 decimals we will get more locked weighted value because we will have much more delta decimals than a token with 18 decimals. The more locked weighted we have value the more daily schnibbles we get 

## Proof of Concept

Example with 6-Decimal Token (USDC)
Decimals: 6
Price: $1
Quantity: 10,000

Example with 18-Decimal Token (ETH)
Decimals: 18
Price: $2,000
Quantity: 5

Let's calculate the lockedWeighted value for both scenarios.

6-Decimal Token (USDC)
Calculate deltaDecimal:

uint256 deltaDecimal = 10 ** (18 - 6); // 10^12 = 1,000,000,000,000

Values:
deltaDecimal: 1,000,000,000,000
quantity: 10,000
usdPrice: 1

Calculating lockedWeighted:
lockedWeighted += (1,000,000,000,000 * 10,000 * 1) / 1e18;

Performing the Calculation:

Multiplication:
1𝑒12×1𝑒4×1=1𝑒16

Division by 1e18:
1𝑒16/1𝑒18=0.01

So, the lockedWeighted value for the 6-decimal token (USDC) is 0.01.

18-Decimal Token (ETH)
Calculate `deltaDecimal:

uint256 deltaDecimal = 10 ** (18 - 18); // 10^0 = 1

Values:
deltaDecimal: 1
quantity: 5
usdPrice: 2,000

Calculating `lockedWeighted:
lockedWeighted += (1 * 5 * 2,000) / 1e18;
Performing the Calculation:

Multiplication:
1×5×2,000=10,000

Division by 1e18:
10,000/1e18=0.00000000001

So, the lockedWeighted value for the 18-decimal token (ETH) is 0.00000000001.

Summary
6-decimal token (USDC): lockedWeighted value is 0.01.
18-decimal token (ETH): lockedWeighted value is 0.00000000001.

In this scenario, even though both tokens have the same total value (price * quantity = $10,000), the lockedWeighted value is significantly higher for the 6-decimal token due to the impact of deltaDecimal. This example highlights how the decimal scaling affects the lockedWeighted calculation, making tokens with fewer decimals contribute more significantly.

# Vulnerability details

In the `unlock()` and `_lock()` functions in `LockManager.sol`, the user-specified token is transfered to/from the user. This `token.transfer`/`token.transferFrom` call's return value is not checked. In the Q&A section on the code4rena description page the following is stated:
`ERC20 used by the protocol:	USDB, WETH, (assume we can add more to the future for use in LockManager)`. Assuming any token might be added to the protocol, also tokens like `ZRX` might be added. Since the returnvalue of the `transfer`/`tranferFrom` calls is not checked as mentioned above, this will lead to problems if such tokens are used.

## Impact
Since some tokens like `ZRX` do not revert on failure when transfering them, users would be able to steal tokens from other users and users' tokens may be locked in the protocol.
Assuming the protocol supports `ZRX` in the future, if a user locks `ZRX` in the contract by calling the `lock` function, the user could not approve these tokens. In that case the `token.transferFrom` call will fail but not revert. Therefore the user's `lockedToken.quantity` will be increased but no tokens are transfered to the contract. If now another user transfers tokens into the protocol, the first malicious user can call `unlock` and since now tokens are in the protocol, they will receive those tokens without ever having depsosited any.

Other scenario: If a user tries to unlock their tokens and the `token.transfer` call fails, this will not be noticed. As the `lockedToken.quantity` is decreased, and the tokens are not transfered to the user but the functioncall ends successfully, these tokens will be locked in the protocol, causing the user to lose their tokens.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add another if-statement like the following, ensuring that the transfer was successful:
(also add a check for the call in `_lock`)
```Solidity
[...]
} else {
    IERC20 token = IERC20(_tokenContract);
    if (!token.transfer(msg.sender, _quantity))
    {
      revert TransferFailed(...);
    }
}
[...]








## Assessed type

ERC20

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L274-L294


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
An attacker can lock his/her funds for a victim player using the [lockOnBehalf() method](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L274-L294).
However, this action triggers the `_lock() method` which reset the `lockedToken.unlockTime`.
Because there is no minimum quantity to lock, an attacker can reset the `lockedToken.unlockTime` of a victim indefinitely. This is a DoS attack on the `unlock` functionality of the victim.

## Proof of Concept
The [lockOnBehalf() method](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L274-L294) allows to lock own funds for another address:

```
LockManager.sol#L274-L294

274      /// @inheritdoc ILockManager
275      function lockOnBehalf(
276          address _tokenContract,
277          uint256 _quantity,
278          address _onBehalfOf
279      )
280          external
281          payable
282          notPaused
283          onlyActiveToken(_tokenContract)
284          onlyConfiguredToken(_tokenContract)
285          nonReentrant
286      {
287          address tokenOwner = msg.sender;
288          address lockRecipient = msg.sender;
289          if (_onBehalfOf != address(0)) {
290              lockRecipient = _onBehalfOf;
291          }
292  
293          _lock(_tokenContract, _quantity, tokenOwner, lockRecipient);
294      }
```

This method resets the `lockedToken.unlockTime` of the `lockRecipient` address. Even if the attacker locks 1 wei on behalf of `lockRecipient`, the `lockedToken.unlockTime` is set again at least to `lockdrop.minLockDuration`:

```
LockManager.sol#L382-L384

382          lockedToken.unlockTime =
383              uint32(block.timestamp) +
384              uint32(_lockDuration);
```

So, an attacker can postpone the unlockTime of a victim indefinitely, because the victim will not be able to call the `unlock method` successfully (line 410):

```
LockManager.sol#L400-L411

400      /// @inheritdoc ILockManager
401      function unlock(
402          address _tokenContract,
403          uint256 _quantity
404      ) external notPaused nonReentrant {
405          LockedToken storage lockedToken = lockedTokens[msg.sender][
406              _tokenContract
407          ];
408          if (lockedToken.quantity < _quantity)
409              revert InsufficientLockAmountError();
410          if (lockedToken.unlockTime > uint32(block.timestamp))
411              revert TokenStillLockedError();
```

## Tools Used

Visual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Only a pre-authorized address should be able to lock funds on behalf of another address. So, we suggest to introduce a mapping to track pre-authorized addresses and add/remove methods to manage them.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L311
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L379


# Vulnerability details

## Description
```lockedToken.remainder``` is set to zero(0) when users lock token during non-LockDrop period (that is, ```block.timestamp > lockdrop.end```). This results in wastage of their remainder that could have been used up in the subsequent LockDrop period to mint NFTs.

## Proof of Concept
The following is a detailed step-by-step explanation of the issue.

Let us assume that user X locks 6500 eth Ether during a LockDrop period through the ```lock()``` function:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L297

```
    function lock(
        address _tokenContract,
        uint256 _quantity
    )
        external
        payable
        notPaused
        onlyActiveToken(_tokenContract)
        onlyConfiguredToken(_tokenContract)
        nonReentrant
    {
        _lock(_tokenContract, _quantity, msg.sender, msg.sender);
    }
```
After locking, X has the following data associated:

```
        lockedToken.remainder = 500 ether;
        lockedToken.quantity = 6500 ether;
```

This is assuming nft cost for Ether is 1000 eth (for making calculations simple).

Now, after some time, the LockDrop period ends.

X again locks 100 eth Ether through the ```lock()``` function. However, after this transaction, X has the following data associated:

```
        lockedToken.remainder = 0 ether;
        lockedToken.quantity = 6600 ether;
```
The remainder is set to zero(0)!

To visualize the gravity of this issue, assume the second lock, that X performed during the non-LockDrop period, did not happen. So, X still has the following associated data:

```
        lockedToken.remainder = 500 ether;
        lockedToken.quantity = 6500 ether;
```
That is, their remainder (during the LockDrop period) is preserved. Now, in a subsequent LockDrop period, X would have minted 1 NFT by locking 500 eth Ether (nft cost is assumed to be 1000 eth). This would not be the case now, as now:

```
        lockedToken.remainder = 0 ether;
``` 
To mint an NFT in the subsequent LockDrop period, X has to lock complete 1000 eth. This clearly shows that the remainder, associated with X from the previous LockDrop period, has not carried over to the subsequent LockDrop event, just because X locked 100 eth Ether during the non-LockDrop period.

The root cause of this issue is that remainder is not preserved when tokens are locked during non-LockDrop period.


## Impact
Impact: The protocol would want a functionality wherein the remainder of the locked tokens of users get carried over. This is also evident in the ```unlock()``` function that the ```lockedToken.remainder``` is not set to zero(0) when users unlock their token; the remainder could be used upon subsequent locks. 

However, this is a valid issue that shows this functionality of the protocol is hindered, making it a case of Medium.

Likelihood: Since the users are exposed to both LockDrop and non-LockDrop periods frequently, the likelihood seems High.

## Tools Used
VS Code
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended to handle ```lockedToken``` data separately for the case of non-LockDrop period.
In the ```_lock()``` function, a local variable, ```_prevRemainder```, could store the previous remainder. If non-LockDrop period exists, then:
```
        lockedToken.remainder = _prevRemainder;
        lockedToken.quantity += _quantity;
```


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L311


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Due to the contract's failure to adjust locked balances dynamically based on changes in token values caused by rebasing events, users may experience impermanent loss when unlocking their tokens. This loss occurs because the contract only tracks balances based on the initial quantity locked without considering changes in token values over time.

## Proof of Concept

The protocal teams intends to use USDB/WETH tokens and the contract is to be deployed on Blast L2. Both USDB and WETH yield mode are AUTOMATIC by default.
The `lockManager` contract makes use of internal accounting to track Amount locked by users. When tokens are locked, `they are held within the contract` and the user becomes eligible to receive rewards based on the locking duration and the amount of tokens locked. 

During the lock period, the total supply of USDB and WETH undergoes rebasing events causing changes in the value of individual token balances.

Upon unlocking, the specified original quantity of tokens is transferred back to the user's wallet along with any accrued rewards based on the locking duration and the amount of tokens locked. The tokens may be worth less due to the uncaptured `rebasing effect on individual users` while on lock.

The  contract  fails to account for the impact of rebasing events to individual users who had locked their USDB or WETH tokens on the contract.

## Tools Used
Manual Analysis
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
 Modify the `LockManager` contract to dynamically adjust locked user balances based on changes in token values caused by rebase events.





## Assessed type

ERC20

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L115-L127
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L363-L369


# Vulnerability details

## Details
Each configuredToken has a `nftCost` field that determines the price of an unrevealed NFT in that particular token. I won't get into the details of unrevealed NFTs, their rarity, and how they are minted, as they are out of scope for this audit. However, since `configuredTokens` might not be updated each time the price of the token changes, it creates an unfair market for players.
Consider this scenario:
- The price of ETH is $3,400.
- Alice deposits 1 ETH with `ETH.nftCost` set to 0.1 ETH per NFT ($340) and receives 10 unrevealed NFTs.
- Bob deposits $3,400 and also receives 10 unrevealed NFTs.
- After the end of the `LockDrop` event, the price of ETH rises to $5,000.
Both Alice and Bob received 10 NFTs. Alice spent $5,000 while Bob spent $3,400. Assuming that these unrevealed NFTs `might` have the same value in the market, Alice incurs a loss.

## Proof of Concept

`nftCost` is only updated in `configureToken` function:

    function configureToken(
        address _tokenContract,
        ConfiguredToken memory _tokenData
    ) external onlyAdmin {
        if (_tokenData.nftCost == 0) revert NFTCostInvalidError();
        if (configuredTokens[_tokenContract].nftCost == 0) {
            configuredTokenContracts.push(_tokenContract);
        }
        configuredTokens[_tokenContract] = _tokenData;
        emit TokenConfigured(_tokenContract, _tokenData);
    }


This means that there must be a mechanism for fetching the latest `nftCost` in that `configuredToken`. For example, if `nftCost` is 100 USD and the price of ETH changes during the `LockDrop` event, the nftCost in ETH must also be updated accordingly. this mechanism is not implemented in the codebase.
as we can see [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/main/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L363-L369), `nftCost` is used directly to calculate number of unrevealed NFTs.


## Impact
some players will receive same amount of NFTs as other players at a higher/lower price which creates an unfair market for players.

## Tools Used
- Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
I recommend fetching the nftCost for each configuredToken in USD value using an on-chain oracle.














## Assessed type

Other

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L259
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L265-L267


# Vulnerability details

## Description

In the Munchables game, registered users can lock their tokens for a selected period of time in order to receive Schnibbles (food to grow the munchables) and also earn new Munchable NFTs.

While Schnibbles depend only on the amount locked, to earn new NFTs users must lock their tokens for a minimum duration during the Lockdrop period, as can be seen [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L357) (note that a maximum duration is enforced as well but it’s not relevant to this report). 

Users lock their tokens by calling `LockManager::lock` or `LockManager::lockOnBehalf` , which will call `LockManager::_lock` to actually lock the tokens and enforce a minimum and maximum locking duration if the current time is within a Lockdrop period. If this is the first time a registered user calls the lock functions, the code will set the duration to the minimum value required by the Lockdrop period, as can be seen [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L349-L350).

If users want to specify the duration of their lock, then they can call the function `LockManager::setLockDuration`. According to the README **`The most important thing is that funds cannot get locked forever, people cannot take other people's funds, and that people cannot reduce lockup times that are previously set.`** So we can understand from this description regarding lockup times, that when setting a new duration for locks, this new duration cannot be such that it unlocks the tokens earlier then the current unlock time. Any new duration set by a user can only extend the lock duration (or at least not change it). The error seen [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L260) also reinforces this.

The issue here arises from the fact that this important functionality is broken and users can reduce their lockup times by as much as half. This essentially bypasses the Lockdrop’s minimum duration and users can unlock their tokens at time that is half of the minimum duration the Lockdrop tries to enforce. 

This happens because there is a mismatch in `LockManager::setLockDuration` between the check in the [if statement](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L259) and the actual [storage update](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L265-L267) of the new unlock time. While the if statement checks for `block.timestamp + duration`, the storage updates according to `lastLockTime + duration`. Unless the user calls `LockManager::setLockDuration` in the same block that they call one of the lock functions, `block.timestamp` will always be greater then `lastLockTime`. This allows a user to manipulate and therefore reduce the unlock time. 

Let’s see an example: A user locks tokens for the first time and so their locking duration is set to the minimum which the sponsor stated is going to be 30 days.  The user waits for 15 days and then calls `LockManager::setLockDuration` with a duration of 15 days. Since 15 days have passed and the duration the user passed is 15 days more, a total of 30 days is calculated and the if statement will not revert. When storage will be updated it will take the original lock time 15 days ago and will add the duration of 15 days to it, which will effectively equal to the current time (because remember we waited 15 days before executing the attack). The user now can call `LockManager::unlock` to receive their tokens back before the minimum duration has passed.

The following is a mathematical treatment to prove that an attacker can reduce the lockup time by a maximum of half

1. Consider the if statement condition:

```solidity
uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
```

Using simple notation, we can rewrite the condition as `Td < Tu - Tc` where `Td` is the new duration we pass, `Tu` is the original unlock time and `Tc` is the current time represented by `block.timestamp`.

2. Consider the storage update equation:

```solidity
lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime = lastLockTime + uint32(_duration)
```

Using simple notation, we can rewrite the equation as `Tnu = Tl + Td` where `Td` is the new duration we pass, `Tnu` is the new calculated unlock time and `Tl` is the original locking time.

3. We want the new unlock time `Tnu` to be equal to the current time `Tc` so that we will be able to immediately unlock the tokens. This means we want `Tnu = Tc`.
4. We can represent the current time `Tc` as the locking time `Tl` + a fraction of the original duration that was set which we will call `xTod` where x represents a number between 0 and 1 and `Tod` is the original duration. So we have `Tc = Tl + xTod`  
5. If we combine (2) and (4) into (3), we get → `Tnu = Tc` ⇒ `Tl + Td = Tl + xTod` ⇒ `x = Td/Tod`
6. We want to pass in (1) the minimum duration `Td` that will satisfy the condition so we write `Td = Tu - Tc`
7. We’ll use (4) on (6) and get → `Td = Tu - Tc` ⇒ `Td = Tu - (Tl + xTod)` ⇒ `Td = (Tu - Tl) - xTod`, and since `Tu - Tl` is the original unlock time minus the original locking time which is just the same as the original duration we can write `Td = Tod - xTod` ⇒ `Td/Tod = 1-x`.
8. Apply (7) on (5) and we get `x = Td/Tod` ⇒ `x = 1 - x` ⇒ `x = 0.5`

So we proved that the maximum reduction of the lockup time is 0.5 of the original duration that was set. If we set the original duration to 10 days, an attacker will be able to unlock their tokens after 5 days only.

## Impact

Users can reduce their lockup times by as much as half. Users bypass the Lockdrop enforcement of a minimum duration and unlock their tokens in half the time of the minimum duration. As stated by the README, this is one of the most important functionalities and so should be considered a breaking of core functionality. 

## Proof of Concept

First add the following piece of code to `MunchablesTest::logLockedTokens` in `MunchablesTest.sol` so we will get logs of the `unlocktime` variable as well:

```solidity
console.log("Unlock Time:", lockedTokens[i].lockedToken.unlockTime);
```

Next add the following test function to `MrTester` contract in `SpeedRun.t.sol`:

```solidity
        function test_ReduceUnlockTime() public {
        uint256 lockAmount = 100e18;

        console.log("Beginning run()");
        deployContracts();

        // register me
        amp.register(MunchablesCommonLib.Realm(3), address(0));
        logSnuggery("Initial snuggery");

        // lock tokens
        lm.lock{value: lockAmount}(address(0), lockAmount);
        lm.setLockDuration(30 days);
        logLockedTokens("After initial lock");

        vm.warp(15 days + 1); // move time by half of the 30 days duration
        console.log(block.timestamp);

        lm.setLockDuration(15 days);
        logLockedTokens("Unlock time reduced"); 
        console.log("Unlock time has been reduced by half of the original duration and is equal to the current time");
    } 
```

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Change the if condition in `LockManager::setLockDuration` to:

```diff
	-           uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime
	+           lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].lastLockTime + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime

```

This way the duration will be with respect to the original locking time.


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L261


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users can set new shorter duration times for their locked funds and emit false events.

## Proof of Concept
The `setLockDuration` function has the following if-statement to make sure that no user can set a new lock duration that is before the current unlockTime:

```solidity
    if ( uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime) {
             revert LockDurationReducedError();
}
```

Then the function updates the new unlockTime immediately after like so:

```solidity
    uint32 lastLockTime = lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].lastLockTime;
    lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime = lastLockTime + uint32(_duration);
```

The problem here is that we are using `uint32(block.timestamp)`, instead of the previous lock time that was set, to check if a user is setting shorter durations. This will lead to shorter durations being set.

Let's imagine a user has already locked funds for a certain duration and wants to set a new duration. For example let's say the user currently has:

1) A previous last lock time at 500
2) An initial duration that was set at 1500
3) A current unlockTime at 2000 (500 + 1500 = 2000)

Now let's say the current block.timestamp is at 1900, and the user calls this function again, but with `_duration` being set to 150, lowered from 1500. Plugging in these numbers in the if-statement will not make it revert:

`if(1900 + 150 < 2000) {
    revert LockDurationReducedError();
}`

Now let's go ahead and update the unlockTime again by plugging in the new numbers and see what we get. The new unlock time is now:

lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime = 500 + 150 = 650
650 < 2000

The event in this function will now emit a new duration of 150, and the new unlockTime is now reduced from 2000 to 650.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider changing the `uint32(block.timestamp)` to `lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].lastLockTime` correctly check the user isn't setting shorter duration periods:

```diff
-    if ( uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime) {
+    if ( lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].lastLockTime + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime) {
             revert LockDurationReducedError();
}
```


## Assessed type

Timing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L177-L207


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A price feed role owner can possibly cast a disapprove vote and approve vote in the same USD proposal.

## Proof of Concept
In the `approveUSDPrice()` function, a price feed role owner can cast an approve vote on a USD price proposal even if they already set a disapprove previously because there is no check to see if the `msg.sender` had previously disapproved the proposal. This will potentially cause both `usdUpdateProposal.approvalsCount++` and  `usdUpdateProposal.disapprovalsCount++` to be incremented by the same user.

It's implied that a price feed role owner can only vote once and not have their vote changed because if we take a look at the `disapproveUSDPrice()` function, it checks to see if the msg.sender previously approved or disapproved. If either option was already made, then the function reverts. See code below inside `disapproveUSDPrice()`:

```solidity
if (usdUpdateProposal.approvals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
       revert ProposalAlreadyApprovedError();
if (usdUpdateProposal.disapprovals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
       revert ProposalAlreadyDisapprovedError();
```
The same must be done inside `approveUSDPrice()` function so that a user who previously disapproved a proposal can not decide to approve the same proposal

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider adding a check inside `approveUSDPrice()` to make sure a user did not already disapprove before. Please add to the beginning of the function:

```diff
if (usdUpdateProposal.disapprovals[msg.sender] == _usdProposalId)
            revert ProposalAlreadyDisapprovedError();
```


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L297-L398


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If a user owns enough NFTs and wants to increase his lock, his NFTs will cause an overflow on uint16

## Proof of Concept
When a user calls `lock()` during a Lockdrop event, all of his unused funds are taken in order to calculate `numberNFTs` and ensure that it is not more than what uint16 can handle. But the check is not enough because the number of his NFTs can overflow because of numerous lock increases and not one big lock.

Example:
If `numberNFTs` would overflow if the user deposits e.g. `quantity = 15000`. Alice is allowed to make 2 different deposits of `_quantity = 7500` and not get reverted but her NFTs would have actually overflowed. 

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a check that a user's total NFTs do not exceed `type(uint16).max` not only the current deposit.


## Assessed type

Under/Overflow

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L245-L272
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L311-L398


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When a user calls `setLockDuration` the `unlockTime` of his tokens can be increased more than they intended.

## Proof of Concept
When a user calls `setLockDuration` the `unlockTime` for his tokens is calculated based on their `lastLockTime` which is set only when the function `_lock()` is called.

Lets say Bob wants to call `setLockDuration` in order to increase his `lockDuration` by 1 day. Alice sees this transaction in the pool and calls `lockOnBehalf` with parameters `_quantity = 0, _onBehalfOf = {Bob's Address}`. After Alice's transaction goes through the new `lastLockTime` of Bob's tokens will be `block.timestamp` instead of some time in the past.

Now when Bob's transaction starts executing. 
               `lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime =
                lastLockTime +
                uint32(_duration);`
`unlockTime` will be bigger than it was supposed to be when Bob first called the function because `lastLockTime` will be `block.timestamp` instead of the time Bob locked his tokens.


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Calculate `unlockTime` by passing only the increase in the lock as a variable in `setLockDuration` instead of the total time. Avoid using `lastLockTime` and use the previous `unlockTime` to calculate the new `unlockTime`


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L311-L398


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users can receive less rewards than they were entitled to during a lockdrop event because of wrong code structure.

## Proof of Concept
When a user calls `lock` during a lockdrop event the amount they deposit is used in order to mint a certain number of NFTs and all of the unused funds are saved in `remainder` in order to be used on the next transaction.

If the user wants to increase their lock amount not during a lockdrop event the variable `remainder` is set to 0 even if it held funds before. The variable is declared and is left with its default value of 0 and is only changed during a lockdrop event. Then it is used to set the user's actual `remainder` `lockedToken.remainder = remainder;`

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L344-L379

After consulting with a member of the contract's team they confirmed that this behavior is unintended and `remainder` is supposed to remain the same when there is no lockdrop event.

The issue is also not that uncommon since anyone can add 0 funds to your lock by calling `lockOnBehalf` and reset your `remainder` value back to 0 



## Tools Used
Manual review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
set remainder to `uint256 remainder = lockedToken.remainder` to ensure that the value remains.





## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L311-L398


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The function `_lock` does not account for tokens that have a fee on transfer which results in the contract having less funds than perceived and the user having a bigger `quantity` deposited than they have which can result in the contract being drained.

## Proof of Concept
Alice wants to lock 10 tokens which have a 10% fee on transfer. She calls `lock()` and reaches the point in the code where her tokens are taken: 
       `if (_tokenContract != address(0)) {
            IERC20 token = IERC20(_tokenContract);
            token.transferFrom(_tokenOwner, address(this), _quantity);
        }
        ...
        lockedToken.quantity += _quantity;
`
The contract calls `transferFrom` with the value 10 because that is what Alice sent. But since the token has a 10% transfer fee the contract will receive 9 tokens but Alice will be registered as having 10 tokens.

After when Alice calls `unlock` to get her tokens back with the value 10, the contract will approve the call since Alice supposedly has 10 tokens. # Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L249-L267


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users can shorten their lock time and have immediate access to their funds. Also they can bypass the `minimumLockTime` set by the contract.

## Proof of Concept
The function `setLockDuration()` is supposed to allow users to only extend their current lock time by passing the new duration. The contract treats the variable `_duration` in 2 different ways. The first way is as the total duration of the lock since its beginning and as the duration to add from `block.timestamp`. Because of this differenece users are able to shorten their lock time.

Example:
In the beginning Alice has a lock that has the following properties: `unlockTime` = 10, `lastLockTime` = 0 and the current `block.timestamp` = 6. She wants to change her lock time so she calls `setLockDuration(5)` with the value `_duration` = 5. She passes the check because 5+6>=10

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L256-L258

That allows her to change her `unlockTime` which is then calculated as `lastLockTime + _duration` which is equal to 0 + 5 = 5. As a result her new `unlockTime` is actually in the past and the funds are no longer locked.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-munchables/blob/57dff486c3cd905f21b330c2157fe23da2a4807d/src/managers/LockManager.sol#L263-L267

This can also be done n-1 times to bypass a lock that is n units in the future. 

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change 
 `if (uint32(block.timestamp) + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime)`
to
`if (lastLockTime + uint32(_duration) < lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime)`


## Assessed type

Math

According to the readme, fee on transfer token behaviour is in scope. However, fee on transfer tokens are not handled in the \_lock function

lockedToken.quantity += _quantity;

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
User's tokens can are frozen for extended periods of time without their possible knowledge or control. 

## Proof of Concept

- User calls `setLockDuration` to lock tokens for 5 days
- gas price goes up and tx doesn't execute for 2 days.
- It then executes due to lowered gas price
- Now comes day 5 when user needs her tokens. But she cannot unlock for 2 more days.
- User has some loans and they will get liquidated due to missing collateral.

This is temporary Freezing of Funds which is a high issue. The probability of it happening is medium, because transactions get delayed in the mempool all the time. 

This kind of issue has been confirmed [medium](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-abracadabra-money-findings/issues/225) recently.

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a `unlockTimeLatest` deadline parameter for the locking function. Fill it with some reasonable deadline, eg 1 hour from tx submission time.

Invalid Validation
